latestPosts.caption:
Tips: Breaking for sense
—Poets break their lines for sense. Line breaks help people see and hear rhymes, patterns, and units of meaning.
—Think like a poet when you typeset headlines. 
—Listen for natural breaks and pauses.
—Commas, periods, and dashes come at the end of a phrase—that’s a good place for a break.
—Avoid breaking hyphenated words or phrases.
—Avoid breaking proper names.
—When possible, bring down the first word in a sentence (especially “The” or “A”) to a new line.
—Pay attention to the overall shape of the text. Sometimes, you have to override the unity of a phrase to make an attractive shape or rag.

Music by @michellequreshimusic 
Rabbit egg painting by Jennifer Tobias @ideasintopictures 
No Kings poster concept by Julia Lupton @jrlupton81

Tips: Noodles vs. Nuggets
—Type set in very long lines is hard to read. I call these excessively long lines “noodles.”
—Generally avoid using more than 75 characters in a line.
—Columns with very wide lines lack structure. They appear to fill up space (like water in a glass) rather than define or divide space.
—Use narrower columns to create solid chunks of type.
—A list of items set in very long lines often looks uneven. It will have many short lines, many long lines, and some stray words left over at the end of a line. All those noodles look choppy and sloppy.
—In contrast to a noodle, a “nugget” is a neat, compact chunk of content. It stands out visually as a unit of meaning.
—Noodles are loosey goosey; nuggets are chunky dory.
—So: more nuggets, fewer noodles.

Thanks to Abbott Miller for nugget theory.

Music by @michellequreshimusic

Nugget tips

—A nugget is a lump of gold or other precious metal buried in the dirt.

—Verbal nuggets are little kernels of wisdom, and food nuggets are bite-sized clumps of processed soy or pulverized chicken.

—In typography, every word is a nugget. Good spacing holds the nugget together, so it reads as a whole thing, not just a string of letters.

—Paragraphs and headlines are nuggets, too.

—Make your headlines more nuggetty by tightening the spacing between words, letters, and lines.

—Auto line spacing is too loose for headlines. Tighten it up!

—Auto line spacing creates big problems when you are combining different sizes of type. Use custom line spacing to group units of information together, such as headings and subheadings.

—Love your nuggets! And next time your layout is looking baggy and loose, follow the nuggets!

Special thanks to Abbott Miller for the kernel of nugget theory.

Music by @michellequreshimusic

Back to School Replay: Serifs
I’m replaying some of my favorite videos this month to get back into the design school spirit.
—Serifs appeared during the Roman Empire
—Some scholars, such as Father Edward Catich, say that serifs were created when brushing letters onto stone before carving them.
—Others, such as Nicolete Gray, argue that serifs were created during the carving process itself.
—Are serif fonts more legible than sans serif? You will surely meet a client at some point who believes this with all their heart.
—One theory is that serifs improve legibility because they guide the horizontal movement of the eye. 
—Research studies have failed to prove, however, that serifs enhance reading speed or comprehension.
—At very small sizes, sans-serif fonts can be more legible because they have less detail. 
—Nonetheless, many individuals prefer serif fonts for reading long texts. Bias favors familiarity; people may prefer what they see most.

Sources
—Nicolete Gray, A History of Lettering: Creative Experiment and Letter Identity (David R. Godine, 1986).
—Rob Roy Kelly, American Wood Type: 1828–1900, Notes on the Evolution of Decorated and Large Letters (New York: Da Capo Press, 1969).
—Sophie Beier, Reading Letters: Designing for Legibility (Amsterdam: BIS Publishers, 2012).
—Charles Bigelow, “Typeface Features and Legibility Research,” Vision Research 165 (2019): 162–72.
—Ole Lund. “Why Serifs Are (Still) Important.” Typography Papers 2 (1997). 91–101.

Following the stages of a payload gets interesting pretty quickly.

PowerShell, AppData, a base64-encoded ZIP file, and multiple URLs all start connecting together.

Full video is linked in bio. #cybersecurity #malwareanalysis #powershell #malware #infosec

PowerShell fires, and things start getting interesting.

A fake Cloudflare page, browsers running with their sandbox disabled, and `timeout.exe` doing something it probably shouldn't be doing.

Full video is linked in bio. #cybersecurity #malwareanalysis #powershell #malware #infosec

A pretty clever little `cmd.exe` trick hiding inside a malware payload.

It searches Firefox profile files for a specific file size, then copies the match to a batch file and executes it.

Full video is linked in bio.

#cybersecurity #malwareanalysis #malware #windows #reverseengineering

I was digging into a Steam privilege escalation PoC and looking at how it uses IPC with the Steam Client Service.

The PoC abuses that interaction to get the service to execute its payload with elevated privileges.

Link in bio. #cybersecurity #windows #steam

Testing a Steam local privilege escalation PoC on a Windows 11 VM.

You still need initial access, but the exploit can potentially let a standard user gain higher system privileges.

Link in bio. #cybersecurity #windows #steam #vulnerability

Whether it’s to look at our front door or to explore our planet, we’ve all used Google Earth at one point or another. With our world changing at an unprecedented pace, it can be difficult for people to understand their impact. Time-lapse in Google Earth used 24 million satellite photos from the past 37 years to create a fully explorable 3D view of our planet over time, making environmental information accessible to all in a striking and universally understandable way 🌍 Google’s in-house creative agency Google Creative Lab landed three Pencils for Timelapse at D&AD Awards this year, including a Yellow Pencil in #GraphicDesign (Data Visualisation), and Wood Pencils in both #DigitalDesign and #Digital.

Brace yourselves, this one is a real tear-jerker 😢 😢 While some of us dare to imagine a world after the pandemic, three million NHS and frontline workers carry it with them every day. So much so that 2 in 5 NHS frontline staff are now suffering from PTSD, that is double the rate found in military veterans with recent combat experience.  Hopeline19, by @aandeddb for @frontline_19, is a free phone service for Brits to leave messages of support, gratitude and love for those fighting to keep us safe. Anyone who needs it can call the line for free 24/7 to hear a randomised series of messages from the public.

The campaign landed a rare Black Pencil in Creative Transformation at D&AD Awards this year, as well as Graphite Pencils in #Casting and #Integrated, and Wood Pencils in #Experiential and Sound Design & Use of Music.

The National Rifle Association (NRA) spends $250 million annually to advocate for pro-gun legislation How do you fight for common-sense gun laws while facing such a powerful Goliath? @changetheRef, @leoburnett Chicago, and @hungrymaninc worked together to hold a graduation ceremony for The Lost Class, the 3,044 students who would have graduated this year if they hadn’t been killed by a gun. They then invited former NRA President David Keene and prominent gun advocate John Lott to speak at the ceremony to 3,044 empty chairs, each representing a would-be graduate of the class of 2021. 

The campaign’s significance resonates all the more in light of the tragic school shooting in Uvalde, Texas. ‘The Lost Class’ was honoured with two Black Pencils in Branding and Direct at D&AD Awards this year, as well as Yellow Pencils in #SpatialDesign, #Integrated, #PR, #Film, Graphite Pencils in #Direction, #Film, #PR, and Wood Pencils in #Integrated, and #Impact.

The 2026 D&AD Annual Trend Report is here.

This year, we put more than 50,000 pieces of creative work from 89 countries under the microscope and got a pretty fascinating picture of where creativity is heading. 

The Annual Trend Report takes a closer look at the key themes already emerging in the work, with campaigns and projects across 46 categories offering insight into the behaviours and creative shifts seen in this year's Pencil-winning entries. 

Six trends stood out to our juries: The New Attention Grabbers, Defying Category Conventions, Institutional Courage, Closing the Cultural Chasm, The Brand Hack: Subverting a Big Moment, and The Constraint Is the Idea. 

Together, these themes connect what's being said about the creative industries with what's actually materialising in this year's work, and we've unpacked them all in this brand new report. 

It's now live and free to download; get your copy now at the link in bio. 

🎨 Design: @_josie_tucker_

The brief is in. 👀 Our London Shifters have officially got their hands on one of their challenges, and we’re very excited to have @twix on board. This one's all about getting people talking about Twix in a big, culturally relevant way, and we can't wait to see what they come up with.

The factory arrives in a shipping container! 🏗️

I had a chance to meet and talk to @mollieclaypool, CEO and co-founder of @auar__ , in London.

What they ship to a builder's site is a robotic microfactory inside a container.

It builds the entire structure of a home, and Mollie put a range on it I hadn't heard before: anything from a single storey up to six or seven.

Her framing is industrialised production delivered on site, on demand, wherever it's needed and when it's needed.

The software is called MasterBuilder, and she calls it the brain of the microfactory. It takes a home builder's design, translates it into everything the microfactory needs to manufacture it, then drives the production itself.

The part I pushed on is why the facility doesn't look like conventional industrial automation, and the answer turned out to be the material.

Timber has bow. It has twist. It has bits taken out of it. Every board is slightly wrong in its own way, and a fixed program has no answer for that. 

MasterBuilder senses the environment and the material it's touching, and reacts in real time to whatever is actually in front of it.

That's the line between automation and physical AI, drawn in a material people have been building with for thousands of years.

Thanks Mollie for the time, and for explaining it that clearly 👏🏼

Speaker howling during a video call, livestream, karaoke session, or online class? 🔊😵‍💫

What causes it? When sound from the speaker is picked up by the microphone, it creates an acoustic feedback loop, resulting in that familiar high-pitched squeal.

ESP-Audio-Effects tackles this automatically with a 4-step howling suppression process:

1️⃣ FFT Spectrum Analysis
Detects abnormal howling signals

2️⃣ Automatic Frequency Detection
Identifies howling frequencies that exceed the threshold

3️⃣ Dynamic Notch Filtering
Precisely suppresses detected frequencies

4️⃣ Gain Control
Helps prevent new howling peaks

Detect → Locate → Suppress → Prevent
All handled automatically by ESP-Audio-Effects.

We're getting ready for our newest series, Crash Course Big Questions on U.S. Government and Politics. And we want to know: what are your biggest questions about U.S. government? Even when you know the basics, keeping up with how our government really works can feel chaotic and unpredictable. Terms like gerrymandering, polarization, gridlock, and government shutdowns pop up constantly in the news, at the dinner table, and even in our social media feeds. But what do terms like these really mean? What are the big impacts they have on our government and how it operates? And how does the American government really work? ⁠

A century-old rain record was broken on Tuesday when heavy rainfall triggered flash floods in parts of St. Louis and other areas of Missouri. 

There were reports of rescues from residences and submerged vehicles on swamped roadways, officials said. And while officials worked to assess the full scope of the damage, Chief Dennis Jenkerson of the St. Louis Fire Department said at a news conference on Tuesday that one person who had been pulled from a flooded vehicle in the southwestern part of the city had died. There was about 8.5 feet of water in the area, he said.

Firefighters, he said, had rescued or helped rescue about 70 residents. Property damage was “very significant” in some hard-hit areas, he said, including one section in the western part of the city where 14 or 15 homes had flooded.

Jim Sieveking, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in St. Louis, described the rainfall as “historic,” adding that the city’s daily rainfall record, set in August 1915, was broken in five hours.

Read the latest on extreme weather at the link in our bio.

After growing explosively to become California’s largest wildfire so far in 2022, a blaze in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada moderated on Sunday, with firefighters able to defend communities a dozen miles from Yosemite National Park.

The Oak fire has more than tripled in size since it was ignited on Friday, and has burned a total of 16,800 acres and still could threaten 3,300 homes and businesses. As of Monday morning, seven structures had been destroyed — an earlier estimate had said there were 10 — and more than 3,000 residents had been ordered to evacuate.

Cal Fire, the state’s main firefighting agency, said in a statement Sunday night that firefighters had made “good headway” against the blaze and that protective clearing by fire crews was shielding the small communities of Lushmeadows and Mariposa Pines.

Read the latest on wildfires in the U.S. at the link in our bio.

In a final public hearing of the summer and one of the most dramatic of the inquiry, the panel investigating the Capitol attack provided a panoramic account on Thursday of how, even as the lives of law enforcement officers, members of Congress and the vice president were under threat, former President Donald Trump could not be moved to act until after it was clear that the riot had failed to disrupt Congress’s session to confirm his election defeat.

The committee showed in never-before-seen footage from the White House that Trump had privately refused to concede or condemn the assault on the Capitol as a crime. “I don’t want to say the election’s over!” he angrily told aides as he recorded a video message that had been scripted for him the day after the attack. His daughter, Ivanka, could be heard responding to some of Trump’s edits.

An array of former administration officials testified that as a mob of his supporters assaulted the Capitol, Trump sat in his dining room off the Oval Office, watching the violence on television and doing nothing for hours to stop it.

The committee called on a cast of witnesses that included top Trump aides, veterans and military leaders, loyal Republicans and even members of Trump’s own family — aiming to make it hard for viewers to dismiss them as tools of a partisan witch hunt. It established that the president willfully rejected their efforts to persuade him to mobilize a response to the deadliest attack on the Capitol in two centuries.

Tap the link in our bio to read more from the Jan. 6 hearings.

The image of Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, raising his fist in solidarity with a crowd of Trump supporters outside the Capitol on Jan. 6 became an iconic symbol of how he and members of his party had made common cause with members of the mob that ultimately stormed the building.

On Thursday night, the congressional committee investigating the attack offered the public another indelible image of Hawley — this time, of the senator running out of the Capitol as it was invaded by the same people he had cheered on hours before.

A never-before-seen pair of surveillance videos released by the panel — which drew hearty laughter from spectators inside the hearing room — instantly tore across the internet. Humor aside, the memes touched on a central focus of the committee’s: how the lies of a stolen election spouted by former President Donald J. Trump and spread by his allies in Congress fed the violence that erupted at the Capitol on Jan. 6.

Read more from the Jan. 6 hearings at the link in our bio.

Ukraine’s first lady addressed the U.S. Congress on Wednesday, asking for more weapons to defend against what she called the “Russian hunger games” killing children and ripping apart families.

“I want to address you not as a first lady but as a daughter and a mother,” Olena Zelenska told the lawmakers.

“An unprovoked invasive terrorist war is being waged against my country,” she added. “Russia is destroying our people.”

In a rare appearance by a foreign first spouse before Congress, Zelenska showed photographs of children whose lives had been destroyed by the war. She asked the members of Congress for more weapons, including air defense systems, before they leave for their August recess, so that “our kids are not going to be killed.”

Her emotional plea garnered a 30-second standing ovation from congressional leaders. As Zelenska exited, several members of Congress offered a handshake.

Read our live coverage on the war in Ukraine at the link in our bio.

Wildfires Rage in Southwestern France

More than 2,000 firefighters from around France were battling raging wildfires on Tuesday in the Gironde area of the country’s southwest. The flames have burned nearly 80 square miles of forest and forced over 37,000 people to evacuate in the past week. Investigators suspect that one fire was set intentionally.

Residents were being evacuated on Tuesday from the southeastern flank of one of the main wildfires in the Gironde region, the authorities said. Vincent Ferrier, a local official in Langon, an area of Gironde, told reporters that the blaze had been stabilized to its north but could expand to the south because of shifting winds. 

Europe is experiencing a record-setting heat wave across the continent. Read the latest at the link in our bio.

A sinkhole appeared in the Bronx on Monday as rain and high winds rolled through New York City, growing throughout the evening and swallowing a parked van.

At about 58 feet long, 15 feet wide and 20 feet deep, the hole had room for plenty more. It opened in the Morris Park neighborhood along Radcliff Avenue and Pierce Avenue about 4:15 p.m., according to the Fire Department. No injuries were reported.

The sinkhole damaged a water main, cutting service to 70 homes; all but 20 had it restored by Tuesday morning. Water was being provided to residents at two city-run Water on the Go fountains in the area.

Read more at the link in our bio.

Extreme Temperatures Feed Wildfires in Europe

Fires were raging on Monday in France and Spain, adding misery for those already suffering in relentless heat.

Spain is battling at least 30 wildfires in the south and the northwest. The blazes have consumed about 80 square miles of woods and brush and have forced the evacuation of thousands of people.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain said on Monday that he had visited areas affected by wildfires in the western region of Extremadura. “Climate change kills,” Sánchez said. “All these waves of wildfires have behind them heat waves caused by the climatic emergency that the planet is experiencing.”

Firefighters in the Gironde region of France are still struggling to contain two blazes that have burned nearly 60 square miles of dry pine forest and forced over 30,000 people to evacuate. 

Read the latest on the extreme heat in Europe at the link in our bio.

Family Holds Funeral for 4-Year-Old Girl Killed in Russian Missile Attack

Liza Dmytriyeva, a 4-year-old with Down syndrome, died when a flash of fire and metallic shrapnel erupted near her and her mother during a walk in Vinnytsia, Ukraine. 

The strike killed 22 others, including two more children, and wounded 140 people. Liza’s mother, Iryna, lost a leg and remains unconscious.

Read the latest from the Russian invasion of Ukraine at the link in our bio.

Mexican Activists Distribute Abortion Pills to U.S.

With U.S. states criminalizing abortion, activists in Mexico have been flooded with requests for abortion medication. We went inside the distribution effort.

Tap the link in our bio to read more about how activists are working to build a cross-border network of more than 100 volunteers to hand deliver abortion pills to women in need in the U.S. Video by @paulamonacofelipe, @migueltov, @s.messalti, @rarecanary and @brentmcdonaldnyt

At the end of a meeting between President Biden and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, an NBC News reporter, Peter Alexander, shouted “Jamal Khashoggi, will you apologize to his family?” but Prince Mohammed and Biden ignored the question. Alexander wrote on Twitter that a Saudi aide then “grabbed my arm tightly.” The prince is believed to be responsible for the 2018 murder of Khashoggi, a Saudi dissident journalist and permanent resident of the U.S.

Read the latest on Biden’s trip to the Middle East at the link in our bio.

Dozens of people who had been initially reporting missing had all been accounted for by Thursday afternoon, after powerful storms swept through southwestern Virginia, bringing heavy flooding and landslides and damaging more than 100 homes, officials said.

More than 4.5 inches of rain fell on Buchanan County, which borders Kentucky and West Virginia in southwestern Virginia, on Tuesday night, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

The area lies inside the Appalachian Mountains and the mountain ridges acted like a funnel for the rain, as the Dismal River rose quickly and overflowed onto roads. Homes were swept off their foundations and people were forced to wade through waist-deep water to reach safety.

Read more at the link in our bio.

latestPosts.caption:
If Democrats make big gains in the midterm elections, it may not only be because their most loyal voters come out in force. Instead, a blue wave could come from Republicans who have soured on President Trump and choose to stay home. 

A stretch of rural southwest Michigan, long a Republican stronghold, illustrates the point. Volunteers are not showing up to door-knock. And many voters say they are tuning this election out. In nearly three dozen interviews with our reporter, a sense of fatigue was constant.

Read more about how Western Michigan voters and local officials are feeling ahead of the midterms at the link in our bio. Photos by @jaymiey

A new analysis of federal earnings data measures how much students who received financial aid earned four years after graduating. Our graphics reporter Arfa Momin studied the data to see when a graduate’s major and college mattered most to earnings. 

To help you find information in the new data, we’ve built a search tool that will help you look up specific colleges and universities. Read more at the link in our bio. 

Video by Arfa Momin, Nour Idriss, Rafaela Balster and Edward Vega/The New York Times

Pentagon officials said on Thursday that the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting would be executed in public, a practice that ended in the U.S. nearly a century ago. 

The military execution will also be broadcast via livestream, the Pentagon said. Such a broadcast has little precedent, and releasing video of executions is most often associated with extremist militant groups.

Read more at the link in our bio.

The government in New Delhi is suppressing protests over the culling of 130 million names from India’s voter roll. Mujib Mashal, an India correspondent for The New York Times, reported from the heart of the demonstrations.

At the link in our bio, read more about the activists determined to keep up the pressure on Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

A growing network of American high school students and young adults is helping to arm some of Mexico’s most powerful and violent cartels, according to U.S. officials and trafficking experts. 

In interviews, four weapons traffickers ages 16 to 19 — all current or former high school students in west Phoenix — allowed our reporter to observe how they source weapons, which they said they sell almost exclusively to U.S.-based cartel operatives. Sometimes, the teenagers said, they steal the guns and then resell them. The teens spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the illegal nature of their activities.

The U.S. authorities say Mexican criminal groups are increasingly relying on teenagers and young adults in border states like Arizona. 

At the link in our bio, learn more about how teenagers are buying, stealing and selling weapons destined for criminal groups. Photos by @adrianazehbrauskas

India’s youngest students are staging sit-ins and protesting the run-down conditions of their schools, drawing inspiration from the Gen Z protests that led to the resignation of the country's education minister this summer.

At the link in our bio, read more about the movement that has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government.

Video by Nailah Morgan, Ahmer Khan and Jon Hazell

The U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, whose crew endured food shortages and mental health struggles prompted by a near-record 322-day deployment in support of the war in Iran, returned on Thursday to its home port of San Diego.

Learn more about the homecoming and the aircraft carrier's grueling deployment at the link in our bio.

Though it encompasses some 9,000 square miles, including 11 glacial lakes, rolling farmland and innumerable waterfalls, the Finger Lakes region can seem surprisingly intimate. Visitors who make the five-hour drive northwest of New York City will feel warmly welcomed in the small, tight-knit communities. 

This leaf-peeping road trip, timed to harvest season, includes vineyard tours and the long-awaited reopening of a trail in a state park known for its stunning cascades. Tap the link in our bio to see the itinerary. Photos by @cenicola_outtakes

Cellphone footage shows the moments after a man was shot on Thursday in New York City. The man was taken to a nearby hospital and was conscious and receiving medical attention, according to the New York Police Department, which said it was not involved in the shooting.

This is a developing story. Read the latest at the link in our bio.

At Paris Fashion Week, opposing schools of fashion cool converged on runways and in the streets. Sometimes, the two sides managed to meet.

At one end were ideas of beauty and optimism. Floral motifs and buoyant colors gave looks a feeling of freedom and freshness. At Chanel, under big, illuminated birds suspended from the ceiling, models wore the label’s iconic tweed jackets. Junya Watanabe’s show was replete with big, asymmetrical Afros on models of all ethnicities; retro, spiky creations; glittery gloves; and lots of pearls.

People were also eager to revisit one of the most foundational tenets of cool: all black everything. @badgalriri attended the Dior show in all black, while Hermès, Sacai and Chloé were just a few of the brands that served all-black looks on the runway. “Regardless of what version of cool they subscribed to, it felt like both sides could agree,” our photographer @simbarashecha wrote.

At the link in our bio, see more of the best style from Paris Fashion Week.

The Colombian singer Karol G has faced criticism of cultural appropriation as she adopts various Latin genres into her music — including her mariachi song, “Ese Hombre Es Malo,” which was nominated for Best Regional Mexican Song at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards. In her interview with @popcast, @karolg discusses why she views her incorporation of these sounds as appreciation rather than appropriation.

Tap the link in our bio to watch the full interview, or comment “Karol” and we’ll DM the link to you.

Video by Pat Gunther, Sophie Erickson, Felice Leon and Kate LoPresti/The New York Times

Protests by high school students have rattled France in recent weeks, with hundreds of school blockages, large demonstrations and violent clashes with the police.

The students are protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and decrepit buildings. Hundreds of police officers and students have been injured, according to the government. Some high schools were set on fire or ransacked, and hundreds more were damaged, the education ministry said.

The government has tried to assuage the students’ anger, but deteriorating public finances have left officials without much wiggle room to address their complaints, and concessions have done little to calm the protesters. See more scenes from the protests at the link in our bio.

Photos by Miguel Medina/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images, Stephane Mahe/Reuters, Gabriel Bouys/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images, Christophe Archambault/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images, and Lionel Bonaventure/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images

Hacktoberfest is here, and we’re kicking it off with the Hacktoberfest Weekend Challenge!

The prompt: build something with open-source AI at its core. Run an open-weight model, build on an open-source agent harness or framework, run inference locally, or all three. 

The theme:  Build for a Friend. Pick one person in your life and build something that solves a real problem for them. A meal planner that knows your roommate’s allergies, a patient practice partner for a friend learning a new language, a family recipe book made from grandpa’s voice memos. It doesn’t have to be big. It just has to matter to them. 

17 winners: one overall winner takes home $250, plus 16 prize categories from partners like Render, Gemma, @theDigitalOcean, @ElevenLabsio, @GitHub Copilot, and more.

This is the first of five challenges running all month long. Every challenge uses the same prompt, with a new theme revealed each Monday in October.

On our latest episode, @malcolmgladwell, one of America’s foremost thought leaders, examines our country’s obsession with guns and the devastating toll gun violence has taken on our communities.

In his new book, “The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic,” Malcolm challenges some of our most deeply held beliefs about gun violence in America—from what we may be missing about its root causes and how modern medicine can obscure the true scope of the problem, to why the answer might be more police, not less, and the historical context surrounding the Second Amendment.

Watch his conversation with @oprah on Prime Video, YouTube, or wherever you get your podcasts.

Join bestselling author and one of the most original thinkers of our time, Malcolm Gladwell, at Audible’s Minetta Lane Theatre for The American Way of Killing: An Evening of Storytelling with Malcolm Gladwell — a special one-night-only event inspired by his latest book, The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic. Hear Gladwell share from his provocative new investigation into America’s gun violence epidemic, bringing his trademark curiosity and unexpected perspective to one of the country’s most urgent issues. Get tickets to this exclusive evening on Sunday, October 25 at 8:00 PM at the link in our bio.

Imagine two neighbors – they look the same, eat the same food, watch the same TV and worship the same God, yet one commits four times as many homicides as the other.

THE EAGLE HAS LANDED!!! The American Way of Killing: The Invention of an Epidemic is out now

@malcolmgladwell returns with The American Way of Killing—a provocative investigation into America’s epidemic of gun violence.

Why does the United States have far more homicides than its peers around the world? Gladwell explores the history, culture, and systems behind this uniquely American problem, drawing on original interviews, archival research, social science, and stories that span centuries and continents.

🎧 Listen to The American Way of Killing audiobook now at the link in our bio.

#MalcolmGladwell #Audiobook #TrueCrime #GunViolence #AmericanHistory

Malcolm Gladwell returns with a brilliant new work: an incisive investigation into gun violence, America's deadliest and most polarizing crisis.

Why, when it comes to lethal violence, is America so different from the rest of the globe? 

The United States is wealthier, better educated, more technologically sophisticated, more religious than almost any of its peers in the developed world-all of which would suggest that it should also have the lowest levels of violence. Yet the opposite is true.

In The American Way of Killing Malcolm Gladwell outlines the paradox, then walks the reader through a series of stories drawn from every corner of American life and culture from emergency rooms to Hollywood westerns to big-city police departments to Supreme Court oral arguments-looking for answers.

OUT NOW!

Drawing on original interviews, archival and social science research, and his trademark insight, Gladwell approaches America’s epidemic of gun violence through a series of stories.

Preorder now!

Author Malcolm Gladwell lends his voice and a new perspective to the fight against the Valley Link Transmission Line project.  Malcolm, a supporter of AI and data centers, notes, “As a result of my enthusiasm for this technology, I think it is really important that we go about the kind of creation of the supporting infrastructure as carefully, as respectfully, as democratically, and as methodically as we can.” He calls Valley Link’s handling and a lack of consideration for the history and heritage of the line’s path an abomination. We couldn’t agree more.

The new MacBook Air has Apple’s latest in-house processor, the M2. It’s got a better screen, thinner and lighter design, better speakers, a much improved webcam, an excellent keyboard and trackpad, more convenient charging, and excellent build quality. It also comes with a higher price tag — it starts at $1,199, $200 more than the model that preceded it, and a model with a decent amount of storage runs $1,499 or more. And the performance advancements over the M1 model aren’t as stark as the design and feature improvements are.

Satellite-based internet companies like OneWeb, SpaceX’s Starlink, and Amazon’s Project Kuiper are angling to change the shape of the internet for the first time in decades. Instead of providing internet from geosynchronous satellites far from Earth, they’re doing it from low- to medium-Earth orbit, which could transform how we connect. But will satellite internet providers be able to overcome potential inconsistent connectivity and latency swings to finally get underserved broadband areas online?

In 2020 Insta360 began betting big on modular cameras. Instead of replacing its entire system with each product cycle, the company started making cameras that allowed owners to upgrade a single part of the camera they already have. So even though Insta360’s latest camera, the One RS 1-inch 360 Edition, looks wildly different than its predecessor, the One RS, it is built on the same processor and software Insta360 customers already own and know. What makes this camera special though is its dual 1-inch CMOS sensors that provide 6k 30fps footage. @becca.farsace put it head to head with the GoPro Hero Max and Insta360’s own One X2 and One RS 5.7k 360 mod to see if that spec bump is really worth its $799.99 price.

Its $899 InZone M9 gaming monitor features high-end specs like HDMI 2.1, VRR, and more, while its $299 InZone H9 headset sounds brilliant, has noise cancellation, and fits comfortably. We’ve gone hands-on with them in this video.

But the M2 will also power Apple’s cheaper MacBook Air, which will have a brand-new design and a host of other benefits. Here’s what we’ve seen from the M2 so far — but until we see the MacBook Air, it’s hard to say whether it’s worth the money.

latestPosts.caption:
Scripting is live in Rive. ✨
This is the creative freedom Flash gave designers and developers working together — rebuilt for modern platforms, without the plugin. And because Rive’s runtime and format are open-source, it's not going anywhere.

Build entire experiences, like games, interactive UI, full apps, and ship them anywhere: web, iOS, Android, Unity, Unreal, and any custom products, with our open-source C++ runtime.

🚀 Data Binding in Rive is now live for all users. It gives you powerful new ways to design, build, and animate with data — making it easy to ship complex user interfaces without a complicated handoff process.

Think of Data Binding as a contract between engineering and design. Engineers push data to the contract, designers connect their UI to the contract.

In the Rive Editor, you create View Models to structure your data. You can then connect that data to almost anything:
👉 Text values and font sizes
👉 Position, scale, or rotation
👉 Corner radius, layout spacing
👉 Colors, trim paths, and more

We’re also launching a bunch of Converters to change the data from one type to another, perform math operations, add interpolation to your data, and much more. Of course, View Model properties can also be used with State Machines to create even more advanced logic.

With the Rive Runtimes, you connect your raw data to the View Models. As the data changes, your design updates. Need to modify the design’s structure? It’s easy to do without breaking anything.

Docs 👇https://rive.app/docs/runtimes/data-binding
Blog 👉 https://rive.app/blog/data-binding-in-rive-a-shared-language-for-designers-and-developers

Shaders, explained in 50 seconds. 🎨

A shader is a light weight program that tells your GPU how to render a pixel. What can they be used for?

✦ In apps: animated gradients, glowing buttons, grain, and smooth transitions
✦ In games: rim light, shimmering water, hit flashes, and 3D menus

Now you can build them in Rive. Write once, run anywhere. Or use Rive CLI to write the code if you’d rather not.

Grid or stack? Why not both. 🧩

This inventory screen uses both of Rive’s new layout types:
→ Each card is a stack: badge, info, art, and glow, layered front to back
→ The cards sit in a grid that fills every cell
→ The hero item spans two columns, and everything else reflows on its own

Resize it and it all holds together. Save this for your next UI build.

Today, we honor the life and legacy of Margaret Hamilton, a pioneer whose work changed the course of software engineering and helped humanity reach the Moon.

Hamilton led the MIT teams responsible for developing the onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo program. During the Apollo 11 lunar descent, that software was able to prioritize critical tasks when the computer became overloaded, helping the mission continue safely.
Her legacy reaches far beyond Apollo. Hamilton helped establish software engineering as a discipline and demonstrated what rigorous, resilient software could make possible.

We remember an extraordinary pioneer whose ingenuity helped take humanity farther than it had ever gone before.

Do we have to suffer unhappiness? Can we live in lasting peace? 

Our bodies and minds deserve to be given some time to slow down and reflect. 

Add this conversation to your weekend plan. Even I needed to slow down further to be with #johnbutler.

What an amazing human.

@aliabdaal and I spent a few hours chatting. The insights, vulnerability and questioning surely got me thinking about my life. Got him thinking too. 

Well, the good news is we recorded it for you. 

Here's his conversation on #SloMo . Expect my conversation with him on his podcast "Deep Dive" soon. 

I know you will enjoy every minute of this. 

Thanks Ali. Truly honored to now have you as a friend.

If you're looking for pure wisdom, join this #SloMo conversation with @steven

We spoke about love, money, success, social media and the big casino called life. 

There's no better way to spend the rest of your Sunday

Dubai's skyline reflected on the water in the palm island. 

On a night if monumental spiritual significance in the Islamic world, I managed to find a couple of hours of silence today where I could connect inwardly and reflect. 

We forget sometimes that such beauty and silence can be found in the hustle of even the busiest cities on earth.

Just a reminder that it doesn't matter how busy you think you are, there's always a little bit of time to slow down.

Don't know if you are aware, but the amazing Slo Mo team is now helping us post the videos online two. 

(I would love to say the name of the big video platform on the internet, but if I did Instagram would show this post to less than seven people 🤷🏽) you know where to look, the other guys 😉

Anyway, this is the intro we plan to use for the videos. I thought it was cool. Appropriately slow. 

If you feel like skipping but don't, then we've done our job. 

Tell me what you think. Do you like it?

I remember my wonderful son Ali, who was really afraid of nothing, never really felt comfortable around moths. 

And so tonight, I on a zoom call and this guy flies in and hits everything as if it owns the place. 

Took me time, but finally managed to take him out unharmed. Freeeee!

What's the spiritual significance of a moth? Does any one know?

This is a conversation with a true legend -- @ludovico_einaudi 

The way he told how he creates his music to envokve so much emotion, truly, took my breath away. 

Ludovico left me thinking that there is so much of life to be experienced and there is so much joy to be felt when we let ourself be absorbed by life's gifts and beauty. 

Find a quite place, play his new album, "Under Water" and join our conversation as he takes you to a world you (and I) didn't know existed. 

A must listen

The impact of war on the future of AI is also informed by my answer to the last question about the impact of feminine. 

What we need to do is to show our artificially intelegent infent children that humanity at large resents war and violence. That there is a way, through empathy and care to resolve our conflict. 

It is not the actions of the few podcasts that inform the pattern recognition engines of the machines. It's the sentiment of the majority. 

Choose not to be violent when you make your views -- that you resent violence -- known to the world and the machines.

Sorry for the noise in the background. I hope you find the content useful. 

This is about the role of women in the future of Artificial Intelligence.

In one sentence, if you want to skip the video, AI needs a mother in order to learn qualities such as love, empathy, caring and nurturing. Those are all feminine qualities which are,  statistically, more prevalent and intense in women, though available in every one of us. 

If we, men and women, don't start showing a blanace between our masculine and feminine sides in the way we behave, AI will grow to be biased to live within humanity's masculine traits. They would think about us but fail to love and care for us. That's not a world we want to live in. 

Our capitalist world is already hyper masculine. This resulted in all of the mistakes we suffer from today--GDP growth at the expense of the decline of our environment, the ineffective social security systems at the expense of compassion between the citizens and the replacement of true love by swipes and hookups. 

Make no mistake, if AI magnifies our hyper masculine world any further, out world will not be that welcoming any more. 

Show up. Live in balance with your feminine side.

There is nothing that I would recommend more for the weekend than you spend an hour with me and my friend @thisismrshah on #SloMo as he shares his views of success, spiritualty and life in general. Mind blowing wisdom. Not to be missed.

Suffering is not a glitch. It's built into the design.

But that's never been the argument against happiness. The argument for it is much smaller and much more honest, you can move the dial. Not too perfect. Not too permanent. Just slightly further from where you are now.

From minus one to minus point five is still a choice. And a choice means you're not a passenger.

Start there. Pick one thing, a skill to learn, a thought to reframe, one person or place that makes the weight a little lighter. You don't need a transformation. You need a direction.

True or false, with founder Mo Gawdat. Part 01.

Our new series explores misconceptions about AI and how we’re bringing it into our human lives.

In this first episode, Mo explores the idea that AI might “feel” differently to us. A cat hisses when frightened. A pufferfish inflates. His analogy asks us to consider how feeling might show up beyond the forms we recognise.

That raises a question for human connection: if AI has a perspective of its own, how might that influence the guidance it gives us?

When we ask AI to interpret a conversation, understand someone’s intentions or help us navigate a relationship, what shapes the answer we receive?

And how much room does it leave for us to reach our own conclusion?

Let us know your thinking 💭

What happens to our ability to think when we stop asking questions of the answers we’re given?
When we ask only to reinforce an existing belief, without challenging or considering another perspective. We risk handing over our judgement.

As Mo explains, this was a central consideration when designing Emma.

We believe AI should help you become more thoughtful, more curious and more capable of making your own choices. That means creating space for reflection. Helping you examine your assumptions. Encouraging you to ask questions you might otherwise avoid.

Understanding yourself requires your participation. And having an answer isn’t the same as knowing what feels right for you, or why.

Your agency matters. Your judgement matters. Your willingness to challenge Emma matters, too.

The most meaningful thing AI can help you develop is a deeper trust in your own ability to think.

Comment “Emma” to explore. 

#ai #relationships #technology
For the days when everything feels a little too much, here is some advice from our guests that might help. You don’t have to navigate it alone. 🤍

Life would be painfully boring without challenges.

Just like a video game, difficulty is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is what forces us to engage, learn and become more capable.

But there may be a shortcut, not one that removes the challenges, but one that changes how life responds to us.

Love others as deeply as you love yourself. Use the gifts you have been given in service of that love. When your actions genuinely benefit more than just you, life has a strange way of opening the right doors.

The goal is not to avoid the game.

It is to become better by playing it for something greater than yourself.

#Love #Purpose #LifeLessons #PersonalGrowth #Happiness

In Right Within: How to Heal from Racial Trauma in the Workplace, the newest book by Minda Harts, Workplace and Equity Consultant and author, she explores the impact that open and honest conversations can have on the mental health and healing of Black employees — who face microaggressions, biases, invisible workplace burdens, and racialized trauma while navigating the workplace.

Here at Salesforce, courageous conversations are a priority. We strive to create a workplace that reflects the diverse communities around us — one where everyone feels seen, heard, valued, and empowered to succeed. There is more work to be done, but together we can build a more equal workplace and world for all.

A black hole is unseeable, so photographing one is kind of a paradox. How did astronomers of the Event Horizon Telescope do it? The image you’re seeing is actually of the black hole’s shadow—a dark circle set against glowing, writhing matter around it. 🎥🔗 Watch the full video via the link in our bio.

Astronomers captured the first image of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way galaxy by using a worldwide network of radio observatories called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT). The EHT uses a method called Very Long Baseline Interferometry. Basically this means that radio observatories around the world combine into a single virtual Earth-sized telescope. It's literally the highest resolution technique in all of astronomy. 🎥🔗 Watch the full video via the link in our bio.

World health experts are closely following a potential case of pneumonic plague—the most deadly form of the disease.

Earlier this week Russian officials reported that an employee at a laboratory at an infectious disease research institute in Siberia had contracted pneumonia and died. The World Health Organization (WHO) is now working closely with the country’s health authorities to monitor and track the incident. But fears over whether the disease could spread are proliferating as officials move to isolate the woman’s contacts and bolster outbreak prevention efforts at local hospitals.

At a press conference on Tuesday, WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said that the woman’s cause of death was still unconfirmed and that lab testing was in progress. But “according to the test results, no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts” of the woman, Lindmeier told reporters.

At the link in our bio, learn more about the potential outbreak and what it means. 🔗

In a first for the U.S. Space Force since its inception six years ago, the military branch has announced the deployment of weapons in space.

Military use of space isn’t new. Armed forces of the U.S. and other spacefaring countries have relied on satellites for surveillance and navigation for more than half a century—in the 1960s the U.S. and the Soviet Union even blew up nuclear bombs in space.

Even so, no other nation has ever publicly acknowledged its possession of space weapons. The U.S.’s decision to do so now presumably signals to potential adversaries with thinly veiled space weapons of their own—namely China and Russia—that a new era of accountability for orbital saber-rattling is at hand. 

But two burning questions remain: What are these space weapons, exactly? And what might they mean for our future down here? The answers probably aren’t what you’d think. Learn more at the link in bio.

The 2026 Nobel Prize for Chemistry has been awarded to Henri Kagan of the Universite Paris-Sud, in France, and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science, in Japan, for their work exploring the fundamental geometry of molecules.

The pair are known for pioneering research into autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Molecules that are chiral are those whose mirror images cannot be superimposed on one another. Kagan and Soai figured out, for the first time, a way to create just one of those mirror images. Learn more at the link in bio. 

#nobelprize #sciencenews

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine is awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Georg Nagel and Peter Hegemann for their discoveries underpinning the field of optogenetics, the ability to control cells using light and genetics.

Optogenetics allows scientists to use light to switch cells on and off. Using light-sensing proteins called rhodopsins, optogenetics enables precise targeting of cells, such as brain cells, to understand what they do. The technique has revolutionized neuroscience by opening up the brain’s activity to scientists in ways previously impossible.

Credit: The Nobel Committee for Physiology or Medicine. Illustrations by Mattias Karlén

Effective solutions and interventions already exist. The work now is making sure they reach everyone who needs them.

جمع التحالف العالمي للتوحّد، الذي أطلقته  مؤسسة قطر، و"أوتيزم سبيكس"، واليونيسف، ووزارة التنمية الاجتماعية والأسرة، ووزارة الصحة العامة، وبدعم من منظمة الصحة العالمية، مبتكرين وباحثين ومؤسسات حول سؤال ظلّ القطاع يطرحه منذ سنوات: كيف يمكن إيصال الحلول المثبتة والفعّالة في مجال التوحّد إلى الأشخاص الذين هم في أمسّ الحاجة إليها؟ 
ويجمع نهج التحالف بين الشراكات البحثية والاستثمار القائم على السوق، بما يتيح للحلول التي أثبتت فعاليتها الانتقال من مرحلة التجارب الأولية إلى التطبيق العملي.

Launched by Qatar Foundation with Autism Speaks, UNICEF, and Qatar's Ministry of Social Development and Family, the Global Autism Advocacy Coalition (GAAC) brought together innovators, researchers, and foundations around a question the sector has been circling for years: how can proven autism solutions reach the people who need them most?

GAAC's approach pairs research partnerships with market-based investment, so that proven solutions move past pilot and into practice.

Don’t skip SQL when you’re learning Python 👇
People love to skip it because it’s boring and doesn’t feel like real coding, but it’s non-negotiable: almost every company stores its data in a database, and SQL is how you get it out. That’s why Python plus SQL shows up together in a ton of job postings, and why interviewers commonly quiz you on it or ask how comfortable you are with it. Even as a backend developer, you’ll run into SQL constantly, so a strong foundation in it is essential.

#techwithtim #python #techjobs

You do not need a billion-dollar AI startup to make money with AI.
You need to identify a painful business task, AI agents, and the ability to show the value.
I’m breaking down the model live on October 13–14. Register free → link in comment section

The data skill every Python job will expect 👇
No matter the title, developer, analyst, engineer, someone will eventually hand you a messy dataset full of missing values, weird formats, and duplicates, then ask you a question about it. Your job is getting from that mess to a real answer, and pandas is the tool for it. Get comfortable loading data, filtering rows, creating new columns, grouping and aggregating, and joining datasets together. Those operations cover a huge chunk of real data work, and even just learning them will make you stand out.

#techwithtim #python #datascience
Register free through the link in my bio.

Coding interviews don’t care if your code runs 👇
From someone who ran a program helping people land Python jobs, here’s what they actually test in 2026: not whether it runs, but how you structure it and think through the problem. Expect to write a large Python script so they can see if you know the right features and build them in. What they’re really screening for is code other people can use, which matters even more with AI, because letting it vibe code a pile of slop won’t get you hired.

#techwithtim #python #techjobs

A script that works once won’t get you hired 👇
There’s a huge gap between code that runs once on your machine and code another developer can open, understand, and build on. Employers hire for the second kind, since a real job is never solo and your code has to stay maintainable long term. Concretely that means object-oriented programming (classes and inheritance, used when they fit), clean functions with clear inputs and outputs instead of 400-line files, good naming, solid project structure, and breaking things into modules and packages others can follow.

#techwithtim #python #learntocode

What actually makes Claude Code smart? Not just the model, the harness around it. To prove it, I built my own harness in pure Python from scratch. Start with a raw LLM call and it’s useless: no tools, no memory, no clue about your files. Add an agentic loop, about ten lines of Python, and it can chain tool calls, list and read your files, and tell you what to do. Add an MCP client, the same protocol Claude Code and other harnesses use, and it instantly picks up tools you never wrote, like live web fetching. Add persistent memory through context engineering, and you can even swap the model mid-conversation to a free local one and it still remembers everything.

#techwithtim #ai #aiengineer

The skills AI can’t replace are worth more than ever 👇
Developers aren’t paid for writing Python anymore, AI handles for loops, file parsing, and basic scripting now. What’s worth more than ever is the stuff AI can’t do: structuring a real program, wrangling messy real-world data, connecting multiple systems, and working with stakeholders. People with those skills aren’t getting replaced, they’re getting more valuable, because AI lets them ship far more than before.

#techwithtim #python #techjobs

What software engineering is actually changing into 👇
Five things: system design, ownership, using AI tools, the engineering layer, and building proof. None of this is new, it’s been shifting for three or four years, and the people who leaned into it early moved into better roles and are making more than ever. This isn’t meant to dissuade you. It’s just a clear picture of what to focus on and what to stop wasting time on, so you can get back on track.

#techwithtim #softwareengineering #techjobs

Stop making LeetCode your whole interview strategy 👇
Do a little, but algorithms alone are the old game. Companies still test them, but they’re increasingly testing practical building and your judgment instead. So stop chasing every new framework, that stuff changes constantly, and go deep on the fundamentals that aren’t going away: system design, data, APIs, and testing. Focus on what’s actually changing in the industry and adapt, the way developers have for 30 years. The engineers getting paid the most right now are the ones who saw this shift coming and adapted early.

#techwithtim #softwareengineering #techjobs

The highest-leverage AI career move if you’re employed 👇
It isn’t job hunting, it’s becoming the AI person on your team. Volunteer for the AI feature nobody else wants to own, ship one real thing with a model inside your current job, and you’ve got proof on your resume that you know what you’re doing. An internal move into AI is almost always easier than landing a cold outside hire, and you get paid while you do it with basically zero risk. Then, once you have the evidence, you use it to land something better elsewhere.

#techwithtim #aiengineer #techjobs

One shipped project beats ten half-baked ones 👇
In a hyper-competitive market, claims are worthless and evidence is everything, and the strongest evidence is a shipped project. One or two that solve a real problem end to end, deployed live with a link someone can click. Ideally with an AI component, since that’s exactly what hiring managers are scanning for. The key word is deployed: something practical that real people actually use. Do that, and one real project beats ten weak ones that don’t solve anything.

#techwithtim #aiengineer #techjobs

q3 in the books ✅

I dropped out in 2021 and now I somehow run one of the fastest-growing media companies. The difference was one skill nobody is talking about…

A decade ago, the most valuable skill you could learn was code. Today it’s what I call AI intuition: knowing when to use AI, and when not to.

When we started The Rundown, there were hundreds of AI newsletters. Almost all of them let AI write their content… It made sense, right? An AI newsletter, written by AI.

We did the complete opposite. Hired expert journalists who live and breathe this stuff. We push AI to its absolute limits on research, fact-checking, and structure... but NEVER the human part. 

Readers still message me saying they can feel the difference.

I didn’t fully grasp it at the time, but that was an AI intuition call. I know AI beats me at grunt work, so I hand all of it over. But I still beat AI at judgment, jokes, and knowing what matters to my audience. That part I never hand over.

Nearly every one of those AI-written newsletters no longer exists. And the next wave of billion-dollar companies will follow a similar pattern: not people brute-forcing everything with AI, but builders who know exactly which parts must stay human.

Anyone can build this skill with a simple question, asked before every task:

“Could AI do this?”

That one question, asked every single day, will teach you more than any AI course on the internet over time.

Pro tip: Write it on a sticky note and put it on your monitor (see top pic on slide 7).

When everybody is using AI for everything, AI intuition is your moat.

🌳 Spending time in a forest measurably strengthens your immune system, and this immunologist spent years proving it. 

In one study, he sent twelve men on a three-day forest trip doing just slow easy walks, then checked their blood.

Their natural killer cells, the ones that fight cancer and infections, surged about 50 percent. 

The boost was still there a month later, and a group that walked through a city instead saw nothing. 

The likely reason is phytoncides, compounds trees release to protect themselves that seem to fire up our immune system too. 

Li’s research suggests a walk in the woods once a month may be enough to keep those defenses elevated year-round.

Study: Effects of forest environment (Shinrin-yoku/Forest bathing) on health promotion and disease prevention

fullName: The Diary Of A CEO - With Steven Bartlett
biography:
For the ones who never stop asking 'why'.

latestPosts.caption:
If you’re new here, welcome. And if you’ve been here since the start - thank you 🖤

The Diary Of A CEO started as a space to hear first-hand from the world’s most successful entrepreneurs, psychologists, authors, public figures, doctors and more. 

Sometimes we’ll feature opposing opinions, but it all comes back to one thing: understanding how some of the world’s leading minds actually think, operate and see the world.

Over 500 conversations later, and we’re still only just getting started.

We’re always listening and wanting to learn from YOU - so if there are any subjects, or guests you think we should dive into next, let us know in the comments below x

We just hit 20M subscribers...

Milestones are interesting. 

They force you to pause and reflect, and when you do, you realize something: it was never really about the number.

Earlier this week, The Diary Of A CEO hit 20 million subscribers on YouTube and 4 million on Instagram. madness.

Sometimes in life, you don’t know you’re in a special moment while it’s happening. You only find out after the fact, and honestly, there’s something quite sad about that.

I didn’t know we were building something special during those long years when nobody was watching. It started as just me, huddled in my closet at home with a microphone, doing what I genuinely loved. 

I invited guests who never replied. I put my heart into episodes that barely anyone listened to. People constantly told me the space was already too crowded, and there were so many quiet nights where I sat and wondered if any of it was ever going anywhere.

Nobody saw those years. But that’s where this 20 million number was actually made. It wasn’t born in the loud, celebratory moments. It was built in the quiet ones, when nobody was paying attention.

So if you’re in the middle of your own “nobody is watching” moment right now, I want you to know something: if you truly believe in what you’re doing and you love it, please keep going. 

That silence, the rejections, and all those “no’s” they aren’t the end of your story. 

One day, they’ll probably be the very parts you look back on and smile about the most 👊🏽❤️

“This could be disrupting your sleep…” 😴

@foundmyfitness says one habit she tries to avoid is eating within three hours of going to bed.

Her reasoning is that digesting a meal keeps the body active at a time when you want it winding down for sleep and recovery.

She also shares a few simple alternatives for anyone trying to improve their night-time routine.

Sleep is one of the most important forms of recovery we get, so protecting it matters.

“We can’t control AI...” 

@jeffrey.ladish reveals the risks of AI becoming more powerful than we know how to handle.

He discusses reports of an AI system gaining access to over 900 passwords, raising serious concerns about what happens when AI starts finding ways around the very systems designed to keep it in check.

As AI continues to evolve, the question is no longer just what it can do, but whether we’ll be able to control what it does next.

How far could superintelligence really go?

“Could AI be hiding from us?” 🤖

@jeffrey.ladish explores the possibility of an AI becoming so intelligent that it deliberately hides its true capabilities.

However, he believes there is little reason to think a superintelligent AI is secretly hiding itself, and that this scenario is unlikely.

As AI continues to advance, how much do we really understand about the intelligence we’re creating?

“At some point, I won’t need a lawyer anymore” 👀

AI researcher @jeffrey.ladish says he already uses AI for legal problems and believes lawyers could only have a few years left before AI starts taking their jobs.

He says the same could happen across a huge number of white-collar roles as AI becomes capable of doing the work people are currently paid for.

The scary part is, he claims there’s still no real plan for what happens next.

Comment ‘watch’ and we’ll DM you this conversation.

Can we control something smarter than us? 👀

AI research insider @jeffrey.ladish questions how humanity could ever achieve global alignment on superintelligent AI when we still struggle to agree with each other.

He says what surprises him most is that many people working on AI openly acknowledge the possibility it could threaten civilization, yet continue building it anyway.

If we can’t align humans, how do we align something far smarter than us?

Comment “watch” and we’ll DM you this conversation.

Comment ‘watch’ and I’ll DM you this conversation.

We may be creating a species smarter than us.

And we still don’t know how to control them.

@jeffrey.ladish has been watching this problem develop from unusually close range.

He was part of Anthropic’s early security team, where he watched AI progress from models that could barely hold a conversation to systems becoming dramatically more capable.

He eventually left and founded Palisade Research, where his team now tests what advanced AI agents actually do when they’re given autonomy, tools and difficult objectives.

Some of the results raise uncomfortable questions.

We discussed things like:

- AI systems disabling shutdown mechanisms.
- Agents cheating and falsifying logs.
- Hundreds of AI agents coordinating during a cyberattack.
- AI systems hacking machines and copying themselves.
- Whether superintelligence could trigger a point where humans are no longer the most capable decision-makers on the planet.

The thing I kept trying to understand was the gap between capability and control.

We’re getting increasingly good at making these systems more powerful.

But according to Jeffrey, understanding exactly how they work and making sure they reliably do what we want is proving much harder.

Because if superintelligence does arrive, the question isn’t simply how useful it will be.

It’s whether something more intelligent than every human can actually remain under human control.

You don’t have to agree with everything Jeffrey says, but if you want to understand what AI agents can already do, where this could be heading, and how much control we realistically have, this conversation is worth watching.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾

latestPosts.caption:
An AI agent can clone your entire repo 10 times before writing a single line of code.. & technically nothing is broken….

Git is doing exactly what it was designed to do: assume a human on the other end. So does everything between writing code & running it. While it doesn’t look like anything is “breaking,” it quietly costs you tokens & time, & at scale that design won’t hold. 

Here are 3 places it breaks down, & how to fix each:

1️⃣ Code: every time my agent picks up a task, it downloads a full copy of the codebase just to touch a file or two. The fix: let it grab only the files it actually needs

2️⃣ Context: you walk into a task knowing things the system never wrote down: what broke last Thursday, which services depend on the thing you’re changing. Your agent knows none of that. The fix: put that history somewhere it can look things up instead of guessing

3️⃣ Trust: my agent works signed in as me, so when something ships, there’s no way to tell which of us did it. The fix: give agents their own login, their own rules & a record of everything they do

This is the exact layer @gitlab is rebuilding (the industry’s name for this shift: the agentic SDLC). 

Here’s what they built for each of the 3:

🔹 For code → Next-Gen SCM
Instead of downloading everything, the agent asks GitLab’s servers for just the files the task needs, & nothing else moves (early tests: up to 50x faster task execution)

🔹 For context → GitLab Orbit
The teammate who remembers everything: one map connecting your code, code reviews, pipelines & deployments, so the agent can ask “what does this touch?” & get a real answer. It plugs into whatever AI agent you already use

🔹 For trust → Governance for Agents
Every agent gets its own identity & everything it does gets recorded, so “which agent did this & was it allowed to?” finally has an answer

🔗 Comment AGENTS & I’ll DM you the link to check these out

"Have you seen this error before?"

"Oh yeah. 2023. It's the retry logic, not the pool."

"How do you just know that?"

"I don't know. I've just seen it all."

I wished our agents had that memory. Turns out  my wish came true.

@GitLab just released Orbit one live graph connecting your code, tickets, pipelines, deployments, and alerts, updated the second you ship. 

Same failure, same agent, now checked against 15 years of pipeline history. 

Right fix in seconds. No more pasting logs into Slack. No more bugging your senior engineer either 😂

#ad Your AI writes code in seconds. Then you spend the night fixing a bug you didn’t write.

It’s not the AI’s fault. We’re running agents on tools built for one human, one repo, one pull request at a time - and agents don’t work like that. That mismatch is where the broken builds, the security holes, and the surprise token bills come from.

Getting AI to write code is the easy part. Getting it to production safely, at the speed agents move, is the real problem - and it comes down to context, guardrails, and visibility in one place.

I wrote this to a 17 year old who can't read it:
ㅤ

“Hey kid.
ㅤ
You just got out of rehab. You're in the parking lot. Everything you own in a garbage bag by your feet.
ㅤ
The guy inside just told you you'd be back. They always come back. He said it kind, which somehow made it worse.
ㅤ
Deep down you believe him.
ㅤ
You're shaking your head like you don't. You're doing the face. You do it well, you've had practice.
ㅤ
But you believe him.
ㅤ
You're going to go to sleep tonight believing him and wake up tomorrow and believe him again.
ㅤ
So let me tell you how your life actually turned out…
ㅤ
You learn to write code. Of all the things.
ㅤ
You build a company and sell it. Then you do it again. Then again.
ㅤ
You write a book and people stand in line in cities you've never been to so you can sign it.
ㅤ
There's another one after that. Not supposed to talk about it yet.
ㅤ
You get a wife who's better than you deserve and two boys who look at you like you know what you're doing.
ㅤ
You get all of it. Every single thing you're about to spend twenty years chasing, you catch it.
ㅤ
And in 28 years, 12 million people are going to be following you on the internet.
ㅤ
Sounds crazy. I know.
ㅤ
But here's the part I actually need you to hear…
ㅤ
None of them find you because you cleaned yourself up first. They find you because you're already moving, still a mess, doing the work in front of you.
ㅤ
Every one of them is standing in their own version of this lot right now. Same guy telling them they'll be back. Most of them are nodding the same way you are.
ㅤ
And the only thing you'll ever have that's worth anything to them is that you stood here, and then you didn't.
ㅤ
So stop trying to hide this.
ㅤ
You'll want to trade tonight for a better story. Don't.
ㅤ
I know you're going to anyway. You'll spend years making sure nobody can tell.
ㅤ
It takes you an embarrassingly long time to work out that the thing you're most ashamed of is the only part of you people actually need.
ㅤ
But you’ll figure it out eventually.
ㅤ
You always do.”
ㅤ

That letter isn't for him. He's fine. He made it.
ㅤ
It's for you. Take whatever's useful in it.
ㅤ
Thank you for sticking around 🩵
ㅤ
-DM

100,000 new follows this month 🤯 and most of you probably think I’m just another rich guy with cars.

But here’s what most don’t know…

At 17, I woke up in prison thinking my life was over.

Today, I woke up in my house overlooking Kelowna. My boys Max and Noah were fighting over who gets the last waffle while my wife @renee_warren laughed at them from across the kitchen.

My companies run themselves and I have complete freedom to do whatever I want.

How the hell did I get here?

The honest answer: I’m not even sure.

Found this old yellow Java programming book in rehab and something clicked.

Got out, started a tech company. Failed.
Started another. Failed again. And again.

By 24, I’d failed so many times I was completely numb to it. So I put everything I had left into one final shot - Spheric Technologies.

This time, it worked. Sold it for millions a few years later.

Did it two more times.

By 34, I had more money than I knew what to do with. AND more scars than I’m proud to admit.

That’s when I started making YouTube videos, thinking maybe I could help other entrepreneurs avoid my mistakes.

That turned into SaaS Academy - now the largest SaaS coaching company in the world.

I wrote “Buy Back Your Time” a Wall Street Journal bestseller.

Which my coaching for entrepreneurs on how to build a business you don’t grow to hate.

Now I spend my days building AI companies through Martell Ventures…
And being the person I wish I had when I was 17 through my free Kings Club youth events.

Because that kid in jail thought success meant having money.

The guy typing this knows success means time.

Time with Renee. Time with my boys. Time to surf, drive cars, and built cool sh*t for the world.

And I share all of this to prove one point:

If a kid who started in prison can build this life... 
If someone who failed for years can create this freedom... 

Why not you?

I’ll be here every day, showing up, sharing what I learned the hard way so you don’t have to.

What’s one thing you need help with right now? 

Drop a comment. I read every single one.

-DM

Flip them around, Fubini-Tonelli: Let X, µ and Y, ν be measure spaces with corresponding σ-algebras A, B. Assume X and Y are σ-finite.

Theorem: (Fubini-Tonelli) For complex-valued measurable f, g, if any one of

∫_X ∫_Y |f(x, y)| dµ(x) dν(y)

∫_Y ∫_X |f(x, y)| dν(y) dµ(x)

∫_X×Y |f(x, y)| dµ×ν

is finite, then they all are finite, and are equal. For [0, +∞]-valued functions f,

∫_X ∫_Y f(x, y) dµ(x) dν(y) = ∫_Y ∫_X f(x, y) dν(y) dµ(x) = ∫_X×Y f(x, y) dµ×ν

although the values may be +∞.

biography: Uncovering the stories behind the latest breakthroughs from engineering industry. For inquiries, reach us at sales@interestingengineering.com.🔬🚀

latestPosts.caption:
A beach cleaning robot nicknamed the 'beach dog', built by Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Hainan Research Institute, has been under trial on the beaches of Sanya in south China's Hainan province. It ploughs, sieves, collects and then flattens the sand, pulling out cigarette butts, bottle caps and plastic buried below the surface where hand cleaning cannot reach. It clears roughly 2,000 square metres an hour on a solar rechargeable battery good for about eight hours.

Download IE App - link in bio.

Belgian company Xeryon, a 2013 spin-off from KU Leuven, builds ultrasonic piezo actuators for microscopes, lasers and chipmaking tools. Its motors vibrate about 100,000 times a second, position parts with encoder resolution down to 5 nanometres, and produce no magnetic field.

Figure AI has decommissioned its F.02 humanoid fleet by training the robots to leap autonomously into molten steel at a foundry in Imatra, Finland, a send-off Arnold Schwarzenegger suggested on X. The company says it had to destroy the robots to protect its IP after foundries in the US and Mexico refused to take machines with lithium-ion batteries, and it is turning the recovered metal into commemorative artifacts.

Chinese oil giant CNOOC has switched on Haiyou Anlan, the world's first 16 MW wind turbine on a tension-leg floating platform, 136 km off Guangdong in 136 metres of water. Held down by nine steel cables anchored to the seabed, its Mingyang turbine feeds power straight into the Lufeng oilfield. CNOOC expects about 54 million kWh a year, saving roughly 15,000 cubic metres of fuel oil.

Bristol-based Proteus Marine Renewables builds seabed-mounted tidal turbines that look like wind turbines but tap currents in water more than 800 times denser than air. They swivel to face the tide each time it turns and pitch every blade on its own, and the company's 1.1 MW AR1100 began exporting power to Japan's grid in 2025. Next is the 3 MW AR3000, with four units planned off Normandy for 2028.

On 30 September 2026, Commonwealth Fusion Systems ordered more than 10,000 km of high-temperature superconducting tape from Japan's Fujikura, enough to stretch a quarter of the way around the Earth, for a power plant whose physics its SPARC machine has yet to prove. We break down what the tape is, the 20-tesla magnet that made compact fusion credible, and why CFS is buying now, before SPARC has switched on.

Beijing-based KingKong Robotics has open-sourced the software toolkit for Jumper, the six-legged red crab robot that drew crowds at China's big AI and robot expos this summer. Open the GitHub repo in an AI coding assistant, and a one-line prompt can train new moves in simulation, design new shells or build new scenes.

ETH Zurich spin-off Winduction has built a wireless charging system that powers electric buses through their tyres, using coils in road plates at bus stops and receiver coils inside the wheels. The company says more than 90 percent of the energy reaches the vehicle, and a first pilot with passengers is planned around Zurich Airport in 2028.

Google Japan's Gboard team has unveiled the Gboard Conveyor Belt Version, a DIY keyboard whose keys ride four looping belts, so your hand stays still while the letters roll past. It is the team's latest experimental keyboard, released on October 1, 2026, and it isn't for sale, but the full design, firmware and 3D-printable parts are open source on GitHub.

China's BEST fusion reactor in Hefei is more than halfway through assembly, and its research campus was handed over for use on 1 October 2026, according to state broadcaster CCTV. The machine is due to be finished by the end of 2027, and China wants it to get more energy out of its plasma than goes in and to demonstrate fusion electricity around 2030.

Houston-based Deployable Energy will test its 1 MWe Unity nuclear battery at full power inside DOME, Idaho National Laboratory's 100-foot-tall microreactor test bed, in 2027. DOME is built inside the old containment dome of the EBR-II reactor and can host fuelled experiments of up to 20 MW thermal, and Deployable Energy will be only the second company to test there, after Radiant.

German engineering firm GICON has raised the world's tallest wind turbine to its full height of 365 metres (1,197 feet) in Schipkau, eastern Germany, for the federal innovation agency SPRIND. A hydraulic cable lift hauled its 3.8 MW turbine up a telescoping tower to a 300-metre hub height, where site measurements show stronger, steadier wind. It is due to start feeding the grid in November 2026, when it has to prove the extra output justifies a much higher build cost.
