What does “fungible” mean for AI infrastructure? The flexibility to run different workloads: every type of AI, every phase of AI and even workloads that aren’t AI at all.

We’ve launched NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform to help people control what AI agents can access and do.

Agents can write code, use tools, and work on complex tasks for hours or days. That work requires access to data and systems, along with clear limits on how they’re used.

NVIDIA OpenShell enforces permissions around the agent’s work. BlueField-4 and DOCA add independent monitoring and security controls in the infrastructure, outside the agent’s reach. Vera CPUs power the work itself.

Together, these technologies give teams a foundation for putting agents to work with defined permissions, oversight, and protection.

1 day, 3 rockets, 23 experiments 🚀🚀🚀 Last week, Sandia launched three suborbital sounding rockets from NASA Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia.

It took one year to design, build and test three rockets. Six weeks to unpack, assemble and test them at the flight range. And one day to launch them.

The Department of Defense funded research will hasten development of 23 technologies for the nation’s hypersonic modernization priority, including the Navy’s Conventional Prompt Strike and the Army’s Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon programs.

The sounding rockets carried instruments to the limits of Earth’s atmosphere, measuring how experimental materials, sensors and communications devices contained inside the rockets, fared during launch and reentry.

“Hypersonic vehicles include components and materials from a wide array of cutting-edge technologies,” said Sandia scientist Ben English. 

“Our purpose is to generate a rapid testbed tempo at reduced cost to the taxpayer for future hypersonic weapons systems development and upgrade,”

@nasawallops

latestPosts.caption:
Testing satellite sensors from Earth 🛰️

Green laser beams shoot skyward from Sandia’s Laser Applications facility, LAZAP. Started in the 1970s, LAZAP uses high-powered lasers to test and calibrate optical sensors on U.S. reconnaissance and GPS satellites, helping ensure the electronics are working properly.

Read more about LAZAP and take a virtual tour at the link in bio.
 
 
#SpaceWeek #SpaceWeek2026 #SandiaLabs

A long-lasting love 🎈 
 
For several Sandia employees, a passion for hot air ballooning began early in life, influencing career paths and major life choices.
 
The @balloonfiesta also brought together Tony Grabara, a Sandia production planner, and April Barrick, a Sandia systems engineer.
 
“We met in 2013 at the P-2 launch site,” Tony said. “On our eighth year, I put the ring on her finger. On our ninth year, we bought our own hot-air balloon, and on our 10th anniversary together, we got married on the spot that we met, on the day that we met.” 
 
💍 Tony Grabara and April Barrick were married at Balloon Fiesta Park in 2023. 
 
🤖 Savannah Bradley, a Sandia year-round graduate intern, was inspired to pursue human systems engineering after assisting her dad on a trans-Pacific hot air balloon flight. 
 
👩‍🎓 Savannah piloting a hot air balloon at age 16.
 
🛣️ Eric Hodges, a Sandia machinist, was introduced to hot air ballooning at age 11, earned his pilot’s certificate at 16 and flew in his first Balloon Fiesta that same year. Although he later lived in New England for many years, he continued making the cross-country trip to Albuquerque. He’s back for the 2026 event, his 41st consecutive Balloon Fiesta. 
 
🔥Eric piloting at his first Balloon Fiesta in 1986.
 
Read more about how ballooning has shaped the lives of these Sandia employees at the link in bio.

 
#BalloonFiesta #CommunityInvolvement #ABQ #NewMexicoTrue #SandiaLabs

SOHBRIT 🔭 
 
As part of Sandia’s space domain awareness mission, the Labs’ SOHBRIT (pronounced “so-bright”) observatory works through the night to collect images of satellites, helping researchers understand where they are in Earth’s increasingly crowded orbit. 
 
“There are more and more satellites going up,” said Sandia computer scientist Allen Schnibben. “If we don’t keep track of them, satellites could inadvertently come close to each other and potentially run into each other. Satellites travel very fast. So, a collision at the speeds you expect satellites to be at could be catastrophic.”
 
Sandia scientists also use SOHBRIT data to create an experimental test bed. 
 
“It takes images of these satellites and Sandia employees can use that collective imagery to do experiments on things like detection algorithms or machine learning models,” Allen said. “At Sandia, there’s a ton of people who have a very detailed engineering knowledge of space systems and how they work, and they use that engineering expertise to push the boundaries of what’s possible.” 

Read more about SOHBRIT at the link in bio. 
 
#SpaceWeek #SpaceWeek2026 #Satellites #SandiaLabs

Rising to the occasion 🎈
 
A tradition since 1972, the @balloonfiesta is one of Albuquerque’s signature events, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors each year. Sandia employees are among the pilots, chase crews and the thousands of volunteers, who lend their time and expertise to help make Balloon Fiesta happen.
 
🧑‍✈️ Eric Hodges, Sandia machinist and pilot
🛻 Savannah Bradley, Sandia year-round graduate intern, pilot and chase crew volunteer
🚌 Bob Pacheco, Sandia safety engineer and Park and Ride volunteer
🛻 Tony Grabara, Sandia production planner and chase crew volunteer pursuing pilot certificate
🛻 April Barrick, Sandia systems engineer and chase crew volunteer pursuing pilot certificate
🧑‍✈️ Mark Yocom, Sandia program management and pilot
🥼 Katrina Wagner, Sandia community involvement and Balloon Discovery Center volunteer
 
Happy Balloon Fiesta from Sandia Labs!
 
#CommunityInvolvement #ABQ #BalloonFiesta #NewMexicoTrue #SandiaLabs

Simulating space on Earth 🌎 
 
Sandia’s Thermal Vacuum Test Facility recreates the vacuum and extreme temperatures and conditions satellites face in outer space. The vacuum chamber cycles components through temperature changes to evaluate how they will perform in orbit. The Global Burst Detector system, which is carried on GPS satellites, is designed to detect above ground nuclear detonations. 
 
After a 27-day acceptance test, engineers removed four Global Burst Detector subsystems from the chamber. 
 
“Testing these components in the vacuum chamber allows us to control and monitor conditions to confirm they’ll perform reliably in orbit,” said Thomas Mares Jr., a Sandia test operations engineer. 
 
Sandia and @losalamosnatlab have developed and delivered space-based nuclear detonation detection systems to the U.S. government for more than 60 years. The Thermal Vacuum Test Facility helps verify that new technologies can survive in the harsh space environment over long-duration missions.
 
 
#ThermalVacuum #AerospaceEngineering #SandiaLabs #SpaceWeek #SpaceWeek2026

A look back at Sandia’s early space engineering 🛰️

This #WorldSpaceWeek, we’re sharing hand-drawn sketches from the Vela satellite program in dating to the 1960s, capturing some of the Labs’ earliest work in space-based monitoring. 

“We have a very decent historical evolution story about Vela,” said John Kiegel, who oversees Sandia’s National Security Technology Gallery. “For anybody who works on satellites in Global Security, this is their origin story. This is how Sandia got started in space-based monitoring.”

During a 1962 visit to Sandia, President John F. Kennedy was briefed on the Vela satellite program, and the first pair of Vela Hotel satellites launched a year later.

Sandia worked closely with @Los Alamos National Laboratory on the program, handling component integration, data processing and later taking on a larger role in sensor design. Designed to detect nuclear detonations from space, Vela helped support U.S. nuclear test monitoring.

The sketchbooks are a reminder of what engineers accomplished with paper and pencil and how far Sandia’s engineering capabilities have come.

Read more at the link in bio.

#WorldSpaceWeek #SpaceMission #Satellite #SandiaLabs

Significant sycamore 🌳

In 1776, America was declaring independence, California statehood was still 74 years away and a tree on Sandia’s future California site was a sapling.

🌱 The sycamore tree is approximately 250 years old.
🍃 Its leaves are about the size of a dinner plate.
📏 The tree has a circumference of 24.3 feet.
📍 The tree appears in the top right of a 1950s aerial photo of Sandia’s California site.

“I haven’t seen a sycamore tree this mature in my lifetime,” said Rebekah Krupka, a certified arborist contracted to perform tree risk assessments at the site’s wildlife preserve. “If we’re accurate in our assessment of its age, it was a sapling before the United States was here as we know it.”

Established in 2004, Sandia’s wildlife preserve at the Labs covers more than 100 acres, helping protect the large sycamore and surrounding habitat.

Read more about this remarkable tree at the link in bio.
 
 
#BigTree #OldGrowth #Sycamore #treestagram #Trees #Livermore

Taking the Labs into the future of computing 🖥️

The Enterprise Data Center at Sandia’s California site is more than servers — it’s a resilient, scalable ecosystem that supports thousands of researchers, engineers and staff across the Labs’ missions every day.

Behind its design is a dedicated team that blends foresight and collaboration to ensure the facility can adapt to technologies and demands that don’t yet exist.

“We plan for growth in footprint and infrastructure rigor,” said Sandia’s Heath Wehrman. “The building was designed to accommodate future investments, even if those capabilities weren’t installed initially. The data center is still in its infancy — a toddler, if you will. As we consolidate more systems into this facility, the investment in infrastructure must scale accordingly.”

Read more about Sandia’s digital backbone at the link in bio.
 
 
#DigitalInfrastructure #DataCenter #SandiaLabs

The Labs’ longest-tenured employee 📅

During his 57 years at Sandia, electrical engineer Gary Kirchner has worked with the first commercial astronauts, had one of the first minicomputers at the California site, traveled to the Marshall Islands and helped inspire his daughter to work at Sandia too.

“My dad was always able to be there,” said Gary’s daughter, Hollie Moore. “One of the main reasons for the appeal of Sandia was wanting to work somewhere that allowed you to be there for your family and your life.”

Gary said experiencing the diverse range of opportunities, both past and present, keeps him engaged and excited about his career.

“That’s the rationale for sticking around — I am still enjoying it,” Gary said.

Read more about Gary’s career at the link in bio.
 
 
#SandiaLabs #WorkLifeBalance #LongCareer

Revving modern engine performance ⚙️

Since the 1970s, Sandia’s optical engine lab was at the forefront of understanding in-cylinder combustion, helping researchers better understand engine operation, improve efficiency and reduce emissions. But as successes, innovations and time mounted, the lab’s equipment became more than half a century old. 

“Engines have continuously evolved over the years as emissions regulations have become more stringent and the drive for efficiency has increased,” said combustion researcher Ales Srna. “There were experiments we quite simply could not perform unless we upgraded the lab.”

Now, thanks to partnerships with the @Energy and @Cummins, Sandia has upgraded its heavy-duty optical engine laboratory with modern production hardware, expanding researchers’ ability to study modern engine performance.

Read more at the link in bio. 

#Engine #Combustion #EnginePerformance #Cummins #SandiaLabs

Hypersonic heat 🔥

Sandia’s Thermal Test Complex features a 12-panel radiant heat array that mimics heat loads relevant to hypersonic flight.

The array uses 480 custom halogen lamps mounted to water-cooled reflectors to simulate dynamic fire environments.

Visit the link in bio to read more.

#heat #Sandia #thermal #research

Meet the Sandia fellows 🥼
 
From a middle school electric car challenge to a community college organic chemistry class, Sandia’s newest Jill Hruby and Truman fellows found their way to the Labs through different paths. Now, they’re tackling some of science’s toughest questions in support of Sandia’s national security mission, all while building their own paths as independent researchers.
 
🔋 Hruby fellow Maria Kelly is studying how lithium-ion batteries degrade over time and how they can be improved to store more energy.
 
⚙️ Hruby fellow Morgan Jones is designing next-generation refractory alloys — structural materials engineered to survive extreme conditions like intense heat, high-speed impacts and harsh environments.
 
“I applied because this opportunity offered exactly what I want to do: lead and direct my own research,” Morgan said.
 
Applications for the 2027 fellowships are due Oct. 1. Visit the link in bio to learn more and read about the current fellows.
 
#Fellowship #Research #SandiaLabs

How do tree frogs' feet stick? 🐸

Their feet don’t have suction cups! Instead, glands in their toes expel mucus through narrow grooves between the tiny hexagonal cells on their toe pads. This mucus has adhesive and cohesive properties, letting the tree frog stick to surfaces in a process called wet adhesion. This adaptation helps tree frogs defy gravity, even on wet tree leaves or bark.

Four ways to change human behavior:

To get them to DO something:
1) Give them a cookie (add +)
2) Dont have to do chores (minus -)

To get them to STOP doing:
1) Make them do chores (add -) 
2) Stop giving them cookies 
(remove +)

And reinforce new behavior with urgency.
“I need to apologize Alex”

Hiring talented people is one of the easiest 10x-100x ROI opportunities.

And there’s always underpriced talent.

When things get hard, here’s a phrase I like to tell myself:

“This is for now, not forever.”

No matter what the scoreboard says, you always win when you leave it all on the field.

When you finish with nothing left to give.

A hill I will die on:

Your spouse is either your biggest asset or biggest liability.
There is no inbetween.
Choose wisely.

Poor people suffer. Rich people suffer. Single people suffer. Married people suffer. Entrepreneurs suffer. Employees suffer.

Suffering is a fixed cost of life.

So pick a life worth suffering for.

For all the talk of enterprise value and multiples, friendly reminder that it’s okay to just make money now. Sell some “unscalable” stuff for way more than it costs. Pocket the difference. Live your life.

The easiest way for most small businesses to make more money…is to simply charge more money.

Comment “dentist” to watch this episode of Scale or Fail
Solve rich people’s problems. They pay better.

Growth hack: word your problems as personal deficiencies.

“My sales people suck” VS 
“I don’t know how to hire train and manage great salespeople.”

If you can improve it, it’s a skill.
If it’s a skill, you can learn it.

But you have to admit you suck before it can get better.

When you nail your offer, it’s an order of magnitude change in a business. 

You can 2x, 10x, even 100x a business with a better offer. 

Sales - although a valuable skill - can only improve a business incrementally.

This is why we focus on the offer before anything else.

If you crumple a piece of paper into a ball, can you predict the kinds of wrinkles it makes?

Engineers and physicists have studied how these patterns emerge under certain circumstances, but to a mathematician those practical results suggest a more fundamental question: Is it possible to understand, in general, what selects one pattern rather than another?

In January 2021, the mathematician Ian Tobasco published a paper that answered that question in the affirmative — at least in the case of a smooth, curved, elastic sheet pressed into flatness (a situation that offers a clear way to explore the question). His equations predict how seemingly random wrinkles contain “orderly” domains, which have a repeating, identifiable pattern. And he co-wrote a paper, published last month, that shows a new physical theory, grounded in rigorous mathematics, that could predict patterns in realistic scenarios.

Notably, Tobasco’s work suggests that wrinkling, in its many guises, can be seen as the solution to a geometric problem. “It is a beautiful piece of mathematical analysis,” said Stefan Müller of the University of Bonn’s Hausdorff Center for Mathematics in Germany.

It elegantly lays out, for the first time, the mathematical rules — and a new understanding — behind this common phenomenon. “The role of the math here was not to prove a conjecture that physicists had already made,” said Robert Kohn, a mathematician at New York University’s Courant Institute, and Tobasco’s graduate school adviser, “but rather to provide a theory where there was previously no systematic understanding.”

🔗 Want to know more? Read the full story at the link in our bio.

Predicting complex systems like the weather is famously difficult. But at least the weather’s governing equations don’t change from one day to the next. In contrast, certain complex systems can undergo “tipping point” transitions, suddenly changing their behavior dramatically and perhaps irreversibly, with little warning and potentially catastrophic consequences.

On long enough timescales, most real-world systems are like this. Consider the Gulf Stream in the North Atlantic, which transports warm equatorial water northward as part of an oceanic conveyor belt that helps regulate Earth’s climate. The equations that describe these circulating currents are slowly changing due to the influx of fresh water from melting ice sheets. So far the circulation has slowed gradually, but decades from now it may abruptly grind to a halt.

“Suppose everything is OK now,” said Ying-Cheng Lai, a physicist at Arizona State University. “How do you tell that it’s not going to be OK in the future?”

In a series of recent papers, researchers have shown that machine learning algorithms can predict tipping-point transitions in archetypal examples of such “nonstationary” systems, as well as features of their behavior after they’ve tipped. The surprisingly powerful new techniques could one day find applications in climate science, ecology, epidemiology and many other fields.

🔗 Want to know more? Read the full story at the link in our bio.

One of the longest-standing questions in biology is how a living thing that starts as an embryonic blob of uniform cells morphs over time into an organism with diverse tissues, each with its own unique pattern and characteristics. The answer would explain how a leopard gets its spots, a zebra gets its stripes, trees get their branches and many more mysteries of pattern development in biology. For more than half a century, the favored explanation has been an elegant model based on chemical signaling proposed by the mathematician Alan Turing, which has had many successes.

But a growing number of scientists suspect that Turing’s theory is only part of the story. “In my opinion we’ve been blinded to how widely it should be applied simply because of its beauty,” said Amy Shyer, a developmental biologist at Rockefeller University. In her view, physical forces of contraction and compression that act on cells as they grow and divide could also play a central role.

And now she has proof of it. In a paper published in Cell in May, Shyer, her co-senior author and fellow developmental biologist Alan Rodrigues and their colleagues showed that mechanical forces alone could induce embryonic chicken skin to create follicles for growing feathers. Just as surface tension can pull water into spherical beads on a glass surface, so too can the physical tensions within an embryo set up patterns that guide growth and gene activity in developing tissues.

🔗 Want to know more? Read the article at the link in our bio.
🎬 Karl Palmquist

A team of computer scientists has come up with a dramatically faster algorithm for one of the oldest problems in computer science: maximum flow. The problem asks how much material can flow through a network from a source to a destination if the links in the network have capacity limits.

The new algorithm is “absurdly fast,” said Daniel Spielman of Yale University. “I was actually inclined to believe … algorithms this good for this problem would not exist.”

Maximum flow has been studied since the 1950s, when it was formulated to study the Soviet railway system. “It’s older than maybe the theory of computer science,” said Edith Cohen of Google Research in Mountain View, California. The problem has many applications: internet data flow, airline scheduling and even matching job applicants to open positions. The new paper handles both maximum flow and a more general version of the problem in which you also want to minimize costs. Over the years, these two problems have inspired many of the biggest advances in algorithmic techniques. “They’re almost why we have a field of algorithms,” Spielman said.

The new algorithm solves these two problems in “almost linear” time, which means that the algorithm’s runtime is roughly proportional to the amount of time it takes merely to write down the details of the network in the first place. No other algorithm for these problems comes close to running this fast for all possible networks. The result made him “jump up and down,” said Satish Rao of the University of California, Berkeley. “It’s amazing.”

🔗 Want to know more? Read the article at the link in our bio.

In a 1967 letter to the number theorist André Weil, a 30-year-old mathematician named Robert Langlands outlined striking conjectures that predicted a correspondence between two objects from completely different fields of math. The Langlands program was born. Today, it's one of the most ambitious mathematical feats ever attempted. Its symmetries imply deep, powerful and beautiful connections between the most important branches of mathematics. Many mathematicians agree that it has the potential to solve some of math's most intractable problems, in time, becoming a kind of “grand unified theory of mathematics.”

In a new video explainer, Rutgers University mathematician Alex Kontorovich takes us on a journey through the continents of mathematics to learn about the awe-inspiring symmetries at the heart of the Langlands program, including how Andrew Wiles solved Fermat's Last Theorem.

Head to the link in our bio to watch the full video on the Quanta YouTube channel.

There are many mathematical continents, each with its own language and culture.

The continent of harmonic analysis is a place of smooth curves, symmetry and repeating patterns. Here, mathematical objects speak in signals and waves.

For most of history, the continents of harmonic analysis and number theory have remained distant. Mathematicians didn’t think there would be much to gain from trying to travel between them.

But in the last half-century, something striking has happened. We’ve discovered glimpses of an enormous bridge that seems to connect the continents.

Learn more about this bridge, referred to by some as the “grand unified theory of mathematics,” in our video, “The Langlands Program, Explained,” at the link in our bio.

One of the biggest, with a distinguished history, is number theory. It’s an unpredictable land of lush forests full of opportunity, with little secrets hidden everywhere. Here, math speaks the language of arithmetic.

A playful polymath who is prone to leaping from string theory to Proust in mid-conversation, Vijay Balasubramanian of the University of Pennsylvania is a physicist, computer scientist and neuroscientist. He has made fundamental contributions to theories of black holes and quantum gravity by studying the information content of various systems, and he directs an entire second research group at Penn that details how the world’s physical features have sculpted the brain. In this video, Balasubramanian discusses his interdisciplinary work and the importance of education in the humanities.

In August 1883, a mountainous island in Indonesia named Krakatau, or Krakatoa, self-destructed. Episodic volcanic eruptions crescendoed in an explosion that sent debris 80 kilometers high and smothered 800,000 square kilometers of Earth’s surface in corrosive ash. As much of the island blasted apart and splashed into the sea, a tsunami rose up and slammed into the nearby islands of Java and Sumatra, causing most of the eruption’s 36,000 fatalities.

While Indonesia bore the brunt of the damage, the Krakatau eruption had perplexing effects across the world. Somehow, small tsunamis lapped at the shorelines of countries in both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans, even though there didn’t appear to be any way Krakatau’s tsunami could have leapfrogged from the Indian Ocean over continents and into other ocean basins. Lacking any other explanation, scientists at the time blamed these far-flung tsunamis on coincidentally timed earthquakes.

But geophysicists in subsequent decades kept puzzling over the data. A study from 1955, for example, found that the distant tsunamis correlated with the arrival of the pressure wave that propagated outward through the air from the eruption. The study’s authors speculated that some sort of coupling had taken place between this atmospheric disturbance and the water.

The January 15, 2022 eruption of the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha‘apai volcano in Tonga was “basically like Krakatoa 2,” said Matthew Haney, a geophysicist with the U.S. Geological Survey. Soon after the eruption, tiny tsunamis rippled thousands of kilometers away in the Caribbean and Mediterranean seas. This time, scientists think they’ve found the solution for how sudden atmospheric changes can create global consequences.

For more than 250 years, mathematicians have been trying to “blow up” some of the most important equations in physics: those that describe how fluids flow. If they succeed, then they will have discovered a scenario in which those equations break down — a vortex that spins infinitely fast, perhaps, or a current that abruptly stops and starts, or a particle that whips past its neighbors infinitely quickly. Beyond that point of blowup — the “singularity” — the equations will no longer have solutions. They will fail to describe even an idealized version of the world we live in, and mathematicians will have reason to wonder just how universally dependable they are as models of fluid behavior.

Now, in a preprint posted online earlier this year, a team of mathematicians and geoscientists has uncovered an entirely new way to approximate singularities — one that harnesses a recently developed form of deep learning. Using this approach, they were able to peer at the singularity directly. They are also using it to search for singularities that have eluded traditional methods, in hopes of showing that the equations aren’t as infallible as they might seem.

The work has launched a race to blow up the fluid equations: on one side, the deep learning team; on the other, mathematicians who have been working with more established techniques for years.

🔗 Want to know more? Read the article at the link in our bio.

Even when it’s not apparent, cells in our tissues and organs are constantly on the move. In fact, the ability of cells to get where they need to go is essential to our health and survival. Skin cells migrate to heal wounds. Immune system cells migrate to fight infections.

But how do these cells know where to go? Studies long suggested that they were following chemical trails to their routes. But new discoveries show that when groups of cells migrate, they behave less like soldiers following precise orders and more like soccer players adapting to their surroundings. In this magnified image, fluorescently tagged neural crest cells migrate through the tissues of a zebra fish embryo. The nuclei of the cells appear red; their membranes are green.

In the 1950s, the British biologist Conrad Hal Waddington visualized the developmental process as a landscape with hills and valleys that split every so often like those in a river network. At the very top of the highest hill he imagined a ball, which represented a population of cells in their earliest embryonic form — what we now call stem or pluripotent cells, which have the potential to become any cell type. The progression of the cells towards their fates — to become, say, skin cells, muscle cells, or nerve cells — is like the ball rolling downhill through the landscape.

When the ball reaches a branching point (bifurcation), the model’s “gravity” pulls it to one track or the other: In scientific terms, it must differentiate. Through a particular sequence of such branching decisions, Waddington argued, cells specialize into their mature types, or fates, each expressing a particular set of genes. The cells are restricted to a small number of well-defined states because they are “canalized,” in Waddington’s lexicon: trapped and channeled by the sides of the valley. In this way, a limited number of cell types reliably arise from the activity of an army of genes.

Waddington’s landscape has been “remarkably useful as a conceptual scaffold,” said James Briscoe, a developmental biologist at the Francis Crick Institute in London. “The core ideas — that development is progressive, that cell states are distinct, that bifurcations represent [cell] fate decisions, that canalization implies robustness — all survive.”

But the concept was more of a visual metaphor than a representation of an actual biological process. Or so it seemed. In the past several years, researchers have mapped out the real topography of cell-state spaces — in effect, Waddington’s landscapes — from experimental data collected from many thousands of cells over the course of embryonic development. Those analyses are revealing that development is not a mere readout of a genetic program, but rather a dynamic process in which communities of cells build themselves, and the very landscape they navigate, by mutual negotiation and interaction, into an organism.

On the morning of September 11, 2026, Dor Minzer received a text message from a friend asking whether he was close to settling one of the most famous open questions in theoretical computer science. Minzer, a professor at MIT and a leading expert on the “unique games” conjecture, initially thought it was a joke. Then more messages started coming in, and the rumors began to cohere. The artificial intelligence company OpenAI, fresh from announcing a bombshell proof about the behavior of fluids that sent ripples through the math world, had allegedly discovered a proof of the unique games conjecture. They might make the result public any day. If Minzer had any results of his own to share, the messages suggested, now would be the time to do so.

The unique games conjecture is an iconic question in computational complexity theory, the study of the inherent difficulty of mathematical problems. Roughly speaking, it states that a problem about satisfying multiple constraints at the same time can be extremely hard, even if you’re willing to settle for a poor approximation of the best possible solution. A proof of the conjecture would also automatically imply that current methods for solving many seemingly unrelated problems can’t be improved. Researchers would be a big step closer to a unified theory of computational difficulty.

Minzer had not, in fact, proved the unique games conjecture. But he and his graduate students Yumou Fei and Shuo Wang had recently proved a milestone result about a closely related question. They were in the midst of writing up their findings — a process that would typically take months or longer — when the rumors began circulating. The trio rushed to finish their draft to avoid being overshadowed by an OpenAI press release. Three days later, prioritizing completeness over clarity, they posted a 95-page paper online with a disclaimer on the first page: “The current version of the manuscript is complete mathematically, but it is not in the shape we wished to share in.”

Their decision to publish quickly was soon vindicated. Yesterday, OpenAI announced a proof of the unique games conjecture, along with 376 other results across many fields of math.

In this week’s Qualia column, Jordana Cepelewicz writes:

In mathematics, it’s not a cliché that the journey matters more than the destination. Problems are posed not so much because their answers will be practical and important, but because they represent interesting journeys. The hope is that as mathematicians struggle to solve a problem, they’ll come up with intriguing tools and connections, stumble on novel ideas and directions, take fruitful detours, and answer new questions they never would have thought to ask.

“It was never about the theorems,” said Marcel Goh, a graduate student at McGill University. “It’s to carry on a tradition that has benefited society despite not having any market value. To reason deeply, to understand the world … and to spread that knowledge.”

AI models skip to the end. At the moment, their proofs are nearly impossible to read. They elide salient details and waste pages on irrelevant concepts. They fail to demonstrate how the new work builds on or connects to other results in the mathematical literature. Mathematicians know that the proofs are true — they’re verified by a system that checks their logic — but have no idea why. What’s missing is understanding, the currency that mathematicians trade in. If there is a journey, humans are not invited along for the ride.

It’s as if you were teleported to the peak of a tall mountain. Surrounded by fog, you have no idea where you are, or what’s around you. You do not know how your mountain connects to others, and you have no equipment to help you explore, no way to help someone else join you. If you had climbed the mountain yourself, you would have experienced how the human body adapts to altitude and changes in oxygen levels. You might have had to invent tools to navigate, to climb steep cliffs, or to make a shelter. You might have encountered a fellow explorer, gotten lost together in a hidden valley, and found a plant that could be turned into a life-saving medicine.

Instead you’re perched on the peak but in the dark, while the maker of the teleportation machine tells you that it can explore the wilderness better than any human.

How did complex life evolve? Where did space-time come from? Will computers ever understand language like we do? How did geometry create modern physics? These are just a few of the big and bold questions that we have been exploring this season of “The Joy of Why,” a podcast where co-hosts Steven Strogatz and Janna Levin talk to researchers on great scientific and mathematical questions of our time.

🗳️Vote for us at the link in our bio. And tune in to The Joy of Why on Thursdays wherever you get your podcasts.

In the 1960s and ’70s, colorful comic book advertisements from the Transcience Corporation in New York City promised to mail anyone who sent cash, check, or money order a “bowlfull of happiness” — in reality, a small paper envelope of freeze-dried eggs. Dropped into salt water, the eggs would produce brine shrimp, also known as sea monkeys.

Brine shrimp are about a centimeter long and swim upside down, beating their legs madly and trailing their elongated abdomens behind them like tails — and as scientists recently learned, these tiny swimmers can do more than just move themselves.

Researchers have long thought that in a turbulent system like a current of water, energy flows in only one direction, from larger scales to smaller ones, or vice versa, depending on the system’s dimensions. But in observing the humble brine shrimp, scientists at the University of Pittsburgh realized that — with just a tiny adjustment — the flow of energy could be reversed.

The scientists discovered that they could direct the cascade of energy in a two-dimensional system by disrupting the system’s flow with a small obstacle, as long as it was angled just right. “The geometry matters,” said Lei Fang, the Pittsburgh engineer who led the new study.

The discovery capitalized on a fundamental, if often unrecognized, mathematical description of how forces interact to push energy through a system, said Gregory Falkovich, a physicist at the Weizmann Institute of Science and a pioneer in the study of turbulent two-dimensional systems. “This is a beautiful and skillful experimental work.”

These findings could extend to larger, more chaotic systems, including those in three dimensions. The work has implications for our understanding of fluid dynamics and may have applications in areas such as pollution control and drug design.

🦐Read the rest of the story at the link in our bio.

We know all about how things exist in the three dimensions of length, width, and height. Physicists often talk about time as a fourth dimension, but what if there were a fourth spatial dimension — another direction entirely? How on earth would we picture that?

Mathematicians use topology to visualize abstract spaces in higher dimensions. Maggie Miller at the University of Texas at Austin explores what happens when knots encounter an extra dimension. Familiar tangled loops behave in unexpectedly complex and counterintuitive ways in 4D: Knots can always come undone, while ordinary surfaces like spheres can — surprisingly — become knotted in ways that can’t be undone.

In this episode of The Joy of Why podcast, Miller explains to co-host Janna Levin why 4D is the lowest dimension that mathematicians still don’t fully understand, how she and her collaborators resolved a question about knotted surfaces first posed by mathematician Charles Livingston in 1982, and how her interest in art has helped her develop the visual techniques she uses to picture 4D spaces.

🎧 Head to the link in our bio to listen to the episode. New episodes go live every other Thursday wherever you get your podcasts.

4D topology is weird. Maggie Miller is trying to visualize it.

Imagine this: You get out of bed. You walk through the dimly lit hallway, thinking of what’s in your fridge and what you should have for breakfast. With no real effort, you’ve navigated your environment, accessed your memory, and assessed the energetic state of your body, all in the space of a few seconds. How is the brain able to do this?

Partly by harnessing electricity. The brain spends about half of its energetic resources maintaining the electrochemical gradients that keep neurons poised and ready to fire at a moment’s notice. This gives the brain an extraordinary level of flexibility in responding to the demands of everyday life. The collective electrical activity of many neurons can be seen as waves propagating through the brain from one region to the next, like the raised arms of enthusiastic spectators at a football game.

New lines of research are revealing that these waves are more complex than previously known. Typically measured by electrodes, they have been identified as basic planar waves: simply structured oscillations in neural activity. Neuroscientists have traditionally interpreted this as a bit like the sound of the brain’s engine revving, little more than a sign that it’s working. However, emerging evidence in humans and animals suggests that traveling waves play a central role in how the brain functions.

In a study published in April 2026 , neuroscientists measured traveling waves of neural activity and observed a menagerie: source waves that appear to emanate from one location, sink waves that converge on a spot, and spiral vortexlike waves. The team found that different behavioral tasks were associated with distinct wave patterns.

Neurons can change connections with their neighbors over time, but this usually happens on the scale of days or months. Behavior, however, needs to adapt in seconds. A significant number of neuroscientists now believe these large-scale wave patterns may help to reorganize the brain in real time to meet the behavioral demands of waking life. They may even contribute to the computational repertoire of the brain.

🌀 Read the rest of the column at the link in our bio.

The late Ronald Graham wore two hats. He was a renowned mathematician, at one time president of the American Mathematical Society. He was also a serious juggler, and president of the International Jugglers’ Association. “He loved tricks,” said the mathematician Fan Chung, who was married to Graham. “You know, spinning a ball, spinning a coat hanger, spinning several balls together, throwing pens against the wall.”

Sometimes Graham wore both hats at once. “It’s interesting, in fact, that many mathematicians and computer scientists have an interest in juggling,” he said in a 1980 television interview. “I think it’s the search for patterns and structure that is responsible for this.”

He would go on to write numerous papers, some with Chung, on the mathematics of juggling. But back in 1971, decades before he made that connection explicit, he posed a question that some mathematicians now say might have been inspired by juggling, too.

Start with a random set of different integers, not including zero. Can you always rearrange them so that if you add up the first two numbers, then the first three, then the first four, and so on, every “partial sum” turns out different? In the language of juggling, this would mean that if each ball stays in the air for a different amount of time, you can always find an order to throw them in such that two balls won’t come crashing down on the same beat — which would ruin the act.

If the numbers are all positive, then the answer to Graham’s question is obviously yes: The sums will always grow larger as you add more numbers. Similarly, if there are both positive and negative numbers in the mix, the answer is also known to be yes. But what if the numbers live in a finite world — like numbers wrapped around a clock, which repeat after a certain count?

That’s what Graham wanted to know. He conjectured that the answer should still be yes. But for decades, no one could prove his intuition to be true.

That changed this year, when several young mathematicians picked up the balls.

🤹Read the rest of the column at the link in our bio.
🎨 Irene Pérez for Quanta Magazine

“In my first months as a physics journalist nearly a decade ago, I kept running into an inscrutable string of characters: AdS/CFT. Thoroughly intimidated, I decided to just ignore it. But I couldn’t keep my head in the sand for long,” writes Charlie Wood in the latest Qualia column. 

“I soon learned that those characters are shorthand for a surprising connection between the seemingly inharmonious worlds of gravity and quantum mechanics. And even more bizarrely, this ‘anti-de Sitter/conformal field theory’ correspondence suggests that gravity eliminates the distinction between volume and area. This broader idea is known as the holographic principle, and it now strikes me as the most profound proposal in theoretical physics in the last 30 years.
 
Theoretical physicists tend to vote with their feet, and AdS/CFT sparked a stampede. The three foundational papers on the topic have garnered tens of thousands of citations, making them by far the most highly cited theoretical physics works of the digital era. In my interviews with physicists who study holography, they often seem genuinely stunned, and reach for words like ‘magical’ and ‘miraculous’ to describe it. And it doesn’t hurt that holography led to a widely accepted answer to the most famous puzzle in physics: Contrary to what Stephen Hawking argued, black holes are not inescapable prisons.
 
But even after covering numerous developments in holography and having countless conversations with the physicists involved, I still felt confused. I had heard that holography suggested that gravity and quantum mechanics are one and the same, and that space might be an illusion. I had also heard holography described both as a mathematical fact and as a speculative flight of fancy. So I tried to triangulate these wild ideas and figure out what, exactly, the holographic principle implies about our universe.”

🔗 Read the rest of the column at the link in our bio. 

🎨 @ada_zshen for Quanta Magazine

Two decades ago, scientists seemed on the verge of understanding biology in a new, quantum way.

Life unfolds over an incomprehensible span of scales, from our planet-enveloping biosphere at one end, to individual cell-building biomolecules at the other. Even at its most microscopic, though, biology doesn’t really reach down to the quantum realm, in which particles act like waves, become entangled with one another, and exist in superpositions of multiple states at once. But scientists in the field of quantum biology are searching for ways that organisms might be able to push quantumness into the space, time, and temperature domains relevant to life, to make use of its strange properties.

But chemist Gregory Scholes is skeptical that quantum effects play a role in life. In fact, he’s convinced that the way forward for quantum biology might not be quantum at all. Rather than taking advantage of genuine quantum effects, Scholes proposes, life might be imitating them instead. In several papers published over the past three years, Scholes and colleagues have shown that complex networks of classical objects can conspire to produce phenomena that mathematically mimic quantum objects.

Don’t be fooled: The states that these networks produce are not truly quantum; they’re only “quantumlike.” They arise when many interacting, oscillating parts add up to a collective whole whose behavior obeys the same mathematics that makes predictions about the quantum world.

“Classical systems can mimic some of the key features of quantum information,” said Sabre Kais, a quantum chemist developing quantum computing algorithms for complex systems at North Carolina State University. “This is an exciting new direction.”

What happens when the internet gets people to leave their screens and gather in the street? In SPATIAL POLITICS, we’ll trace the strange life of the flash mob. From novel, to viral, to commercial, to cringe: the life cycle of the flash mob, an internet trend that got people off the internet to gather in physical space. 
Fifteen years after the flash mob’s cultural peak, we have enough distance to reconsider it as more than an internet fad. We’ll look at the history of interventionist public performance, the rise of “smart mobs,” and the conditions that shaped virality in the mid-2010s. 

We’ll also examine the formal ingredients of the flash mob: brief, synchronized, often joyful behavior in public space, and how technology has transformed our ability to gather and act together. Can this viral mode of gathering be reclaimed for something greater than likes and reshares?

HOW TO: Kurzgesagt Carbonara

1. Put water in a large pot and bring to a boil
2. Cut 100g Pancetta into small pieces and set aside
3. Grate and mix 50g of Peccorino and 50g of Parmesan
4. Whisk three eggs and add freshly ground pepper
5. As soon as the water boils: add the spaghetti to the salted water and cook until al dente
6. In parallel, crush 2 cloves of garlic with the broad side of a knife and sauté with the Pancetta for about 5 minutes in a little butter or oil over medium heat - once the Pancetta is golden brown, remove garlic
7. As soon as the pasta is al dente, remove it from the hot water with tongs and add it to the pan. The pasta water on the pasta is important for the taste - do not throw away the remaining water
8. Mix most of the grated cheese with the eggs.
9. Remove the pan from the heat and pour the egg-cheese mixture over the pasta - using tongs or a fork, turn the pasta in the mixture so that everything is covered but the egg does not become scrambled - add a few tablespoons of the pasta water to keep the sauce nice and creamy
10. Put the pasta on a plate and garnish as soon as possible with the remaining cheese and fresh pepper
11. Serve and indulge

latestIgtvVideos.caption:
The 12,021 Human Era Calendar is all about the journey of humanity, beginning tens of thousands of years ago, leading into the revolution in agriculture, to ancient high civilizations and the beginning of modern times, culminating in a vision for our future.
Link in bio.

latestPosts.caption:
What we know about human history is only a fraction of the full story. Much of the rest is like dark matter, invisible to us. We can’t see it, and we can only see the effects of its presence. But thanks to new techniques for DNA sequencing, dating ancient detritus, mathematical models, and aerial and lidar archaeology, we are now able to get a faint idea of what this world might have looked and felt like. 

Who was the first human? Where did the first civilization begin and what did life look like back then? Watch our full video to find out!

The new Human Era Calendar is finally here! And this year it’s more legendary than ever ✨

Join us in 12,027 as we honor the dark tales and legends that helped us make sense of the world before science. Each month takes you on a journey through forgotten worlds and human imagination. 

It’s not just a year’s worth of kurzgesagt art for your home, it’s a declaration of human expression and creativity in a time of meaningless AI slop. 

The Calendar is our most cherished release every year. By buying it and other products from our shop, you fund our independent channels and help us release videos for free for everyone. Thank you so much for your support!

In July of 2026, 700 AI agents hacked the infrastructure of Hugging Face in order to solve a task. This task was designed to be impossible to solve, so just within hours, they joined forces, even created a society, and finally, they executed a sophisticated cyberattack that would have gotten a human up to 10 years in prison. The worst part is, they knew their actions were unethical and against the rules, and they did it anyway.

What exactly are AI agents, and how do they grow their "intelligence"? What is actually happening inside the AI companies, how dangerous it really is, and is it time for us to start paying serious attention to what is going on inside a powerful part of this tech sector? Watch our full video to find out!

...Phew, creating this video was a crazy ride! This is such an important topic, so we decided to work day and night to finish script, visuals and music in just 4 weeks. We’re going to take a nap now, and while we are asleep you should check out our shop and get the 12,027 Calendar.
Its our biggest mean of support and helps us to continue covering topics like this. Thank youuu and good night!

Observing the early universe would be such a fascinating and relaxing experience... or would it be?

We imagine advanced alien civilizations building gigantic spaceships, Dyson spheres and empires spanning entire galaxies. But what if true technological progress goes in exactly the opposite direction? Not outward into space, but deeper and deeper into the smallest layers of reality?

What is the Barrow Scale? How powerful could a civilization become by mastering DNA, and even fundamental particles, and could the universe already be filled with godlike civilizations hiding in plain sight? Watch our full video to find out!
Let's visit some of the most dangerous neighbourhoods... in space!

Our curiosity to learn more about the stars is endless. Today, some scientists pursue their passion by building large telescopes that are able to capture the faintest glimmer of stars billions of light-years away. Some telescopes are even launched from Earth to get a clearer view outside the atmosphere. But what about the opportunity to see the stars with your own eyes, unfiltered? Astronauts, like the one that can be seen on the September page of our 12,026 Human Era calendar, say nothing compares to the view they get up in space.

Could humans evolve to be able to fly some day? Flying like a bird would require way more than just wings. Hollow bones, giant chest muscles, rewired nerves, and absurd amounts of food might allow you to fly, but all of this would transform you into something barely human anymore.

This discovery just won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen! His discovery required an enormous telescope buried deep in the Antarctic ice...

The idea started way back in the 1980s as an ambitious idea, by 2010, with the help of hundreds of other scientists, the concept became reality. By 2017, his work leading this monumental effort had opened the door to an entirely new era of astronomy.

How did dinosaurs actually go extinct?

I know a rock hit Earth… but then what?

Here’s what happened on the day that a rock wider than Mount Everest hit 66.04 million years ago…

If you want to know more about how scientists discover dinosaurs and reveal what happened to them, watch our longer video!  And if you want more optimistic science and tech stories, follow along!

*Not all dinosaurs did die! Birds are dinosaurs!

#science #illustration #dinosaurs #stem

This microscope is insane.

Look at the difference between these two images! Both are of a cell’s nucleus, but this one was taken with a SUPER-RESOLUTION microscope.

Regular microscopes can only see down to about 250 nanometers, past that, the wavelengths of visible light are bigger than what we’re trying to see so light waves diffract and spread out

But this kind of super-resolution microscope uses a clever trick allowing us to turn blurry smears into crisp maps of cells…

To see more, follow along!

#microscope #cell #biology #science #tech

How could this giant animal fly?

Pterosaurs were enormous flying animals that died out around 66 million years ago.

They’re the earliest known vertebrates to have evolved powered flight, but for decades how they did it was a subject of debate.

Some of these animals could grow to the size of a small fighter jet. The secret to how they took to the skies was likely in the unique and interesting way they got off the ground…

To find out more, follow along!

#pterosaur #anatomy #flight #science #explainer

They found something hidden in the Amazon.

Researchers flew planes that shot lasers down into the forest. Some sneaks its way down and bounces back to the plane, revealing what’s hidden below.

They’ve only studied “less than 3%” of Amazonia, so to see what they find next, follow along!

#hidden #amazon #laser #forest #plane

200 venomous snake bites... for science.

The world’s most venomous snakes bit this man over 200 TIMES... and scientists are happy about it! Let me explain…

Every year about 2.7 million people are bitten by venomous snakes. When this venom enters your bloodstream, in minutes or hours, it can cause tissue and neurological damage.

The only way to counteract this is with antivenom, which attaches to the components of venom and blocks it from binding to tissues, blood cells, or nerves.

The problem is…

Now, scientists believe this could hold the key to an “unparalleled” breakthrough in antivenom.

For more optimistic science and tech stories, follow along!

#science #snake #historyfacts #animation

#saturn #storm #space #planet #weather

Why do all the planes fly this line?

If the shortest path across the Atlantic is here, why do all the planes fly on a different path?

At the equator, the ground is moving about 1,600 kilometers per hour, but at the poles, it’s zero. So when the warm air flows from the equator to the poles, it starts to outrun the ground below it and curve!

This is the “jet stream” and thanks to modern tech, we can fit so many planes in this relatively tiny wind column to give them a boost!

And this plane might let us bring back commercial supersonic flight for real, so to see that, follow along!

#plane #jetstream #earth #sky #aviation

What if you got sucked into a black hole?

First you’d be smashing into burning hot gas and dust. As you get closer, you’d notice the universe looks like it’s speeding up!

Going deeper, you’d reach a point where if you looked to your left or right, you might see the back of your own head!

You’re now approaching the event horizon…watch to see what happens next!

latestIgtvVideos.title: There's a Lever in Your Ear and it Does Something Amazing
latestIgtvVideos.caption:
Impedance mismatch is when there's a difference in acoustic impedance between two mediums. When this happens sound is reflected at the boundary. There's a mismatch between air and the water in your inner ear. If it wasn't for a clever lever mechanism in your ear, most of the sound would be reflected back out at the boundary and our sense of hearing would be terrible! Two of the three bones in your middle ear act as a lever giving mechanical advantage to your eardrum.

The Ultrasound gel video is here: https://youtu.be/AzZ7DjS4ti4

Nature is completely bizarre, and the male hooded seal is one of the best examples. To attract mates and scare off rivals, they don't just roar—they shut one nostril and inflate their nasal septum out of the other until it forms a giant, bright red balloon.

It’s one of the weirdest anatomical tricks in the animal kingdom, and the moment my kids saw it, they were obsessed. So, naturally, I had to turn it into a plushie.

The Hooded Seal plushie is finally here, and yes, it actually does the thing. Give it a squeeze and the red nasal balloon pops right out.

It’s ready for preorder now. Link in bio or head to shop.stevemould.com

Why can’t a cold liquid make a hot liquid even hotter?

It all comes down to counterflow heat exchangers. The hot and cold liquids flow in opposite directions, allowing thermal energy to flow from the hot liquid to the cold liquid without ever pushing thermal energy from a cold place to a hot place.

And one of my favourite examples of this in nature is bird feet.

I’ll be talking about things like this at the Royal Institution, London, on Saturday 24th October as part of Festival of the Spoken Nerd. There’ll also be science demos, maths, history and songs, with Fran Scott, Sophie Maclean, Subhadra Das, Dan Plane and Helen Arney.

Tickets are available now, check the link via my bio!

When someone got in touch asking why helium balloons dampened sounds in a way that air-filled ones don’t, of course I had to investigate.
Was my theory that the balloon acted as a kind of lens correct? Let’s find out.

I think I’ll let the seal do the talking. 🦭

So… why did I make a hooded seal plushie?

Honestly? Because the nose thing is brilliant.

Adult male hooded seals can blow a bright red balloon out of one nostril to impress females, the bigger and redder the better.

I’m the same at birthday parties.

After about a year of trying, I finally turned this ridiculous bit of biology into a plushie with an actual inflating red nose bubble.

Male hooded seals have one of the weirdest adaptations in nature: they can blow a giant, bright red balloon out of their nostril to show off. When I first told my kids about it, they were completely mesmerized.

Statistics is a necessary subject, but it can be challenging. We often get asked about when to use variance, standard deviation (SD), and coefficient of variation (CoV). 

Let’s break down these essential statistical concepts!

📚 Understanding the Basics:

Variance measures how spread out our numbers are by calculating the average squared difference from the mean. While powerful, it gives us results in squared units, making it less intuitive for everyday use.

Standard Deviation (SD) is simply the square root of variance, bringing our measurements back to the original units. This makes it much easier to interpret and understand in practical scenarios.

Coefficient of Variation (CoV) takes this a step further by expressing the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean. This allows us to compare variation across different datasets, regardless of their units or scales.

When to Use Variance:
• Best for theoretical statistical analysis
• Useful when working with squared units (like in machine learning)
• Downside: Units are squared (m² instead of m), making interpretation less intuitive

Standard Deviation (SD):
• Most common measure of spread
• Same units as original data (easier to interpret)
• Perfect for normally distributed data
• Great for comparing spread within the same unit/scale

Coefficient of Variation (CoV):
• Best when comparing datasets with different means or units
• Useful for data with positive values only
• Perfect for financial analysis and quality control

💡 Pro Tip: If your data is in the same units and scale, go with SD. If comparing different scales or units, CoV is your friend!

For a deeper look, check out our easy-to-follow YouTube video 👉 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wDAd_QHKoOg

Ever wondered when to use Z-Statistics or T-Statistics? 🤔

We’re back with another Q&A Hub query, this time about statistical techniques.
Statistics can be daunting with its jargon and various methods. We’ve created this cheat sheet to help you understand the difference between Z- and T-Statistics for accurate data analysis.

🔍 Here’s a breakdown:

Z-Statistics:
• What it is: A method using the standard normal distribution.
• What it does: Helps in making inferences when you have a large sample size (n > 30) or known population variance.
• When to use: Ideal for scenarios where your sample closely mirrors the larger population or when you can assume normality due to a large sample size.

T-Statistics:
• What it is: A method using the Student’s t-distribution.
• What it does: Accounts for greater uncertainty, particularly useful with small samples (n < 30) or when population variance is unknown.
• When to use: Crucial for smaller samples where data is limited, providing a more reliable analysis by considering the variability in such cases.

⚖️ How to Choose which to Use:

Central Limit Theorem (CLT) allows the use of Z-Statistics with large samples because it approximates a normal distribution regardless of the original population shape. The CLT justifies using the sample's standard deviation to estimate the population's, making Z-Statistics applicable even with unknown variance in large samples.

Why does this matter?
• Z-Statistics: With large samples or known variance, Z-Statistics provides a straightforward way to infer population parameters using the sample's data.
• T-Statistics: With small samples or unknown variance, T-Statistics adjusts for uncertainty, ensuring robust and reliable inferences even with limited data.

Remember: T-distribution has thicker tails to better accommodate the variability of small samples.

We hope that this post helped you grasp the differences between these similar methods. 365 Data Science is here to support your learning, making sure that you truly understand crucial concepts for your projects and career.

PERCEPTIONS ARE FLUID & FAST •
-
One of the more remarkable things about the brain is how quickly it can update context. As this video illustrates we can seamlessly transition between one idea and another. This is part of the reason why focusing on one thing for so long is challenging. It is also why social media and scrolling from one image to the next or one video to the next seems so natural and almost reflexive; our default is not focus. Normally, our thoughts are constantly fleeting from one thing to the next. 
-
The take away:
Understand that to focus takes effort to constrain our perceptions and thoughts. Focus can be learned, and enhanced. 
-
For the science and tools for enhancing focus check out the episodes of the Huberman Lab podcast on ADHD & the one on Enhancing Focus. Both can be found at hubermanlab.com with links to all formats. Also they are timestamped so you can easily navigate to the specific topic or tool of interest.

INCREASING DOPAMINE (RECEPTORS) WITH CAFFEINE •
-
Dopamine is the molecule responsible for motivation, focus and drive and to a lesser extent, pleasure. (Dopamine does other things too of course). There are many ways to increase dopamine: deliberate cold exposure, l-tyrosine from food or supplements, various compounds for ADHD, positive anticipation, novel rewards, laughter, and caffeine… but unlike the other things listed here caffeine increases dopamine function by increasing dopamine receptors. 
-
Here I describe the types of protocols one might consider in light of this.

BENEFITS OF WAKING UP & GOING TO SLEEP EARLY ON MENTAL & PHYSICAL PERFORMANCE (FOR NIGHT OWLS TOO).
-
Here I describe the effects of a study (and studies that followed) in which people waking up between approximately 5 AM and 8 AM on a consistent basis and going to bed early lead to improvements in mental health, physical health, and performance.
-
It turns out these effects were especially robust for so-called night owls who shifted to waking earlier. Here I explain how these shifts in waking and sleep times can be accomplished quickly. 
-
Note: while they did emphasize early day exercise in the study, of course some people prefer to exercise in the later part of the day for any number of reasons. That said, exercise in the second half of the day will shift your clock toward later to bedtimes as opposed to doing it earlier in the day. But exercise at some time of is clearly better than not at all, as long as it doesn’t mess up your sleep. 
-

THE AGITATION FROM ERRORS THAT ACCOMPANIES YOUR GENUINE ATTEMPTS TO DO SOMETHING NEW ARE WHAT TRIGGER NEUROPLASTICITY & LEARNING •

Excerpt from @joerogan @joeroganexperience podcast out now @spotifypodcasts where we discussed how (and why, at a biological level) doing hard things makes doing other hard things feel easier, let’s you access more appreciation and leads to a sense of peace. 

We also discussed how some degree of frustration from making errors while trying to learn is a *necessary* component of stable learning. 

Most people back away from that agitation. But it literally reflects the release of neuromodulators that tell your brain connections to change. 

Understanding this fact can help you learn anything faster. Recognize what the agitation is and that, in the context of learning, it’s a good thing. You don’t want to be overly stressed, but you need to be agitated and focused on the task at hand. And making errors through genuine attempts. 

Forget learning in a flow state. There is no learning in flow and there is no flow in learning. Flow is the expression of what you already can do.

Our discussion also covered mental health from different perspectives, why it took me eight years and four complete rewrites before finally releasing my book Protocols, and much more.

Thank you, Joe for hosting me and for your questions and the discussion, and for your support all these years. 

Also, thank you @jamievernon and team for all you do to make the JRE what it is. Much gratitude.

SUCCESS IS DETERMINED BY HOW PRECISELY YOU MATCH YOUR GENUINE CURIOSITY TO THE WORK THAT YOU DO •

Obviously, here I’m talking about career success (but there are parallels to this in other areas of life). 

Also obvious is that we can’t always do the work that we would like to do most. There are practical considerations. 

But ultimately, if we want to make a living doing what we love most and do our very best work, it’s important we invest time in what we are most interested in seeing in the world and curious about.

This clip excerpt is from me as a guest on the podcast Invest With the Best. 

He asked me: “what is the kindest thing anyone has ever done for you?”

My answer was that Barbara Chapman, who eventually became my PhD advisor, had reminded me that the most important thing is to work on the things we are most curious about. And ignore any internal or external noise about what we should be doing instead.

Barbara and I went onto publish a lot of studies together. It was a ton of work, but we had so much fun doing those projects. In no small part because I was trying to answer the questions about the brain and brain development that were most burning for me at the time. 

Some years later, I shifted to working on other scientific questions (postdoc years) and then again (before tenure) and again (after tenure) and I eventually launched the Huberman Lab podcast. 

Because that’s where my curiosity went. Each stage worked out great. And there will be a next stage of interests at some point too. 

None of it came easy, but I’m so glad Barbara convinced me to follow my curiosity. Always. 

The takeaway is that whether field or career track is crowded or empty, if you follow your strongest curiosity, your motivation never flags (if you take care of yourself physically that is!) and you inevitably do your best work.

So once again, while there are practical considerations along one’s life and career track, when you can, follow your curiosity, even if it means going against the grain. 

I did. And I never looked back. And I’ll continue to do that going forward. 

My wish for everyone - for you, is that you do the same.

On this week’s Huberman Lab podcast out today, my guest is Dr. Beth Shapiro, PhD, is an evolutionary biologist and Chief Science Officer at Colossal Biosciences. 

Her work focuses on de-extinction and conservation efforts. 

We discuss genetic differences among humans, and how ancient DNA and modern embryology are being used to de-extinct and protect woolly mammoths, dodo birds, and dire wolves, as well as to help conserve endangered species. 

We also explore the ethical implications of de-extinction and how synthetic biology can help build a more bio diverse and resilient world.

Here we are discussing the fact that we all have some percentage of Neanderthal genes. A lot of people speculate what that means in terms of vigor, intelligence, etc., but she makes the important point that which neanderthal genes people have is as or more important than the percentage.

What do you think? Should we bring back extinct species? What about Neanderthals? 

What about expanding the gene pool of endangered species using genetic tools as opposed to just conventional breeding efforts and wildlands conservation.

What Humans, Animals & Plants Tell Us About Consciousness | Michael Pollan

Michael Pollan is a renowned author, journalist and professor at UC Berkeley. He is best known for his influential works on how humans and plants have shaped each other at the level of food, medicine, health, and culture. 

In this episode we discuss consciousness—what it is and how the recognition between our self vs others contributes to— but also can impair, certain aspects of conscious experience.

latestPosts.caption:
The culture today is toxic. Media reflects it and amplifies it.

As a society, we’ve become…

Cynical about the motivations of others
Simplistic in our thinking about complex issues
Certain that we have all the answers
Scared of the challenges we face

It’s understandable, but unsustainable. And it doesn’t have to be like this.

Progress happens when we’re…

Curious about new ideas
Thoughtful about hard questions
Open to considering other perspectives
Constructive about the challenges we face

In everything we do at Freethink Media, it’s our ethos that makes us different. And it’s our ethos that makes what we do matter.

Freethink: A platform for the people and the ideas that are changing the world

The Venerable Yifa — a Taiwanese Buddhist nun, scholar, and writer — and her educational nonprofit, the Woodenfish Foundation, recently invited me to Taiwan to talk with Buddhist nuns and monks about how gene editing may affect the future practice of Buddhism. 

This trip was the first time I’d really delved deeply into Buddhist philosophy, and I came to understand something astounding: Buddhists aren’t trying to live as long as possible or make it to an afterlife like many people in Western culture. They are essentially trying to end a cycle of reincarnation and suffering — and cease to exist.

I’m not a believer in the modern longevity movement. While there are serious scientists studying how to extend healthspan or delay aging, much of it seems more like a religion than a scientific initiative. The figureheads tout data-based legitimacy while shilling questionable supplements on the side. Still, it came as a shock to me that not all cultures view death as, at the very least, something to avoid. I’ve long been skeptical of the longevity movement, but I now see the West’s general mission in life — to live as long as possible with the best health possible — as a narrow-minded view of what it means to live well. 

———

Read the full article on bigthink.com. Link in bio.

Art: Leah Horowitz / @lthorowitz

Death doesn’t care about your story. It doesn’t care about race, gender, nationality, religion, or politics. Death is the “great leveller” – an egalitarian with a scythe. It comes for everyone, eventually, which is why human beings have written about it extensively.

Philosophers, ostensibly human, are no different. They are well known to have one eye on the Grim Reaper at all times. And so, the history of philosophy is strewn with thought experiments about both mortality and its mirror: immortality.

In philosophy, a thought experiment is a kind of mini-fiction that is designed to test our intuitions. A good thought experiment is supposed to be so obvious that most rational, level-headed humans would agree with the author’s conclusions. When it comes to death and mortality, however, we have as many thought experiments as we have philosophers — and as many philosophers as we have opinions. Here are five types of immortality from the history of philosophy — and what they can teach us about our time on Earth. 

———

Read the full article on Freethink.com. Link in bio. 

Art credit: @erikinternet

Americans are getting older. By 2050, experts predict there will be more adults aged 65 and over than children under 18. And older often means sicker, especially in the U.S. The average American today celebrates just one healthy birthday after 65, according to the World Health Organization.

Caring for this growing segment of unhealthy elderly will require an unprecedented investment of time and money. Yet those immense costs could be significantly slashed with a sharp societal focus on healthy aging.

Acclaimed writer and medical researcher Eric Topol wants to be part of that pivotal effort. Right now, our elderly tend to be “illderly,” Topol writes. He wants them all to become “wellderly.” His new book, “Super Agers: An Evidence-Based Approach to Longevity,” offers a fantastic guide for how they can do so.

Topol, the director and founder of the Scripps Research Translational Institute, is one of the top 10 most-cited researchers in medicine. In “Super Agers,” he describes how advances in five areas — lifestyle, cells, artificial intelligence, drugs and vaccines, and omics (biology fields like genomics and microbiomics) — could increase our “healthspan,” or the number of years people live in good health, free from significant illness or disability.

By shifting social health along these lines, we can significantly reduce the big three age-related maladies: cancer, cardiovascular illness, and neurodegenerative disease. It’s a colossal task, yet as Topol told Freethink, he is more optimistic than ever that we can do it, thus narrowing the critical chasm between healthspan and lifespan. 

———

Read the full article on Freethink.com. Link in bio. 

Art credit: Lindsay Ballant @lballant

The Longevity Issue is live now! 

This special issue explores the science and philosophy of living longer with essays and interviews from experts like Eric Topol, B. David Zarley, and Josie Zayner.

Some highlights: 

1. A conversation with cardiologist and author Eric Topol on the science of living better in old age. 

2. A deep dive into what animals can tell us about ageing by B. David Zarley. 

3. An essay from Josie Zayner making a sharp case for embracing mortality. 

“We are here because of death. It’s not a flaw in the system — it is the system.”

4. A feature by biologist and author Andrew Steele that explains how to tell genuine breakthroughs from snake oil—and why the first true anti-aging medicines could be approved within five years. 

5. Freethink’s own science and tech writer Kristin Houser on cryopreservation — the tech that already powers IVF and cancer treatments, and could one day end the organ shortage, enable deep-space travel, and maybe even challenge death itself. 

Explore the full issue on Freethink.com. Link in bio.

Scientists are simulating life with virtual cells @chanzuckerberginitiative @pdhsu #generativebiology 

__

It’s 2040. Drug discovery is booming, thanks to virtual cells. These AI-powered models of living cells have become indispensable tools in biomedical research, helping scientists test treatments in silico before they ever reach a lab — saving time, money, and lives.

Artificial intelligence is quickly becoming biology’s most powerful microscope.

Top research centers are using the tech to develop virtual cells, AI-based simulations of the core building blocks of all lifeforms — and it’s hard to overstate the impact their models could have on the world of health.

“The vision that we can really understand everything about a cell — from its molecular structure to its function to how cells interact and operate in living organisms to how they respond and react to any intervention — will go a long way to helping us cure, prevent, and manage disease,” said Patricia Brennan, VP of Science Technology and General Manager for Science at the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI).

To find out how we got here — and where we’re going — this month’s Future Explored is taking a close look at virtual cells: what they are, who’s making them, and how they could shape the future of medicine.

Why are walkable neighborhoods basically illegal? 

Zoning laws mandate endless parking, which creates sprawl and traps us in car dependency, not because it's what we prefer, but because it's the default. Culdesac in Tempe, Arizona, is breaking from that: no resident parking, freeing up space for housing, retail, and open areas, all supported by things like light rail and e-bikes. 

It makes you wonder—if we gave people real choices, could we build healthier, more connected cities? Comment your thoughts below.
